title: Once props
description: Remember expensive values on the client and skip them on later visits.
body: Once props are expensive values that rarely change. The client remembers them across visits and tells the server which keys it holds with X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props . Behavior - The value is left out on later visits, but the onceProps entry stays so the client keeps its copy. - .Fresh() sends the value even when the client has it. - Partial reloads always resolve once props that the reload asks for. - Expiry is computed from the registered TimeProvider , so tests can use FakeTimeProvider . - .As(key) and .Until(ttl) imply once. - Sharing a key between pages lets the client reuse one value across them. Keys The default key is the prop path. Use .As("billing-plans") when the same value is exposed under different names, or when you want a stable key across page changes. Two props that share a key are treated as the same client value. Only share a key when the values are actually the same. When in doubt, use the default prop path. Expiry .Until(TimeSpan) sets expiresAt in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. The client stops treating the key as loaded after that time and requests the value again. The server leaves the value out only when the client lists the key in X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props . Shared once props This is the equivalent of Laravel's shareOnce : the client keeps the value across visits. Testing InertiaPage.OnceProps exposes the metadata: Revisit the page with the same client and assert that the prop is missing while onceProps remains.

title: Build a todo app
description: Build ForgetMeNot step by step with shadcn/ui, covering sign-in, shared lists, infinite scroll, live reminders and server-side rendering, using named routes, typed routes and caching.
headings: 2. Make it look good with shadcn/ui
7. Share a list, and render it on the server
8. A reminder that appears by itself
body: ForgetMeNot is a small todo app. It is small, but it uses the same pieces as a real product: sign-in, private data, a public page, a long list that loads as you scroll, and a reminder that appears on your screen without a refresh. Each step tells you what to do and why . If you know why a line is there, you can change it later without fear. - The .NET 10 or .NET 11 SDK - Bun, npm, pnpm or Yarn. The commands use Bun; swap in your own. - A code editor and a terminal You do not need a database server. The app uses SQLite, a database that lives in one file. What you will build Every feature below is here because it shows one idea from Inertia.Net. The right column says which one. You build You learn --- --- A polished interface shadcn/ui cards, lists, switches and a theme you can change in one place Sign in with a cookie The --auth starter, redirects to the login page, and a sign-in rate limit A page of lists Page records, named routes and the typed routes.ts file A form that checks itself Precognition: the server validates a field as you type Slow numbers that load after the page Deferred props, plus a cache you clear when data changes A list with thousands of items ToPageAsync and infinite scroll A link anyone can open Server-side rendering and the SSR cache A reminder that shows up by itself Live props over SignalR Tests Inertia.Net.Testing 1. Create the app Install the templates once, then create the app. --auth adds cookie sign-in, so you do not write that yourself. Use --framework vue or --framework svelte for the other clients, and pick the matching tab in the examples below. Start the two development processes and keep both terminals open: Open http://localhost:5180 , click Log in , and sign in with demo@example.com and the password password . Click around before you change anything. Vite serves your React, Vue or Svelte code and reloads it the moment you save. ASP.NET Core serves the pages. While Vite runs, it writes a small file called wwwroot/hot , and the app uses it to find Vite. Nothing else is needed. The template is not empty. It already uses the features we want, and it is worth knowing where they are: Where What it does Why it matters --- --- --- HomePage , LoginPage in Program.cs Page records. A record that names its component once: Component = "Home" The props and the page name stay together, and the compiler checks them .WithName("login") on each route Named routes A name is a stable handle for a URL. You can change the URL and nothing breaks ClientApp/types/routes.ts Typed routes , written from the names In the browser you write routes.login() , never the string "/login" ClientApp/types/inertia.d.ts TypeScript types for every page, written from the C records A renamed property is a compile error, not a blank spot on the page .WithInertiaPrecognition() on the login The form checks a field on the server when you leave it One set of rules, run in the browser and on the server AddInertiaErrorPages() A 404 or 500 shows your Error page Visitors never see a raw error Both generated files are rewritten when the app starts in Development. You never edit them by hand. 2. Make it look good with shadcn/ui The template's pages have almost no styling. We will use shadcn/ui , a set of well-made components: cards, inputs, checkboxes, switches, lists and more. They are built on Tailwind CSS, and they are copied into your project , so you own the code and can change any of it. First, Tailwind CSS and an @ shortcut for imports (so you write @/components/ui/button instead of ../../components/ui/button ): In vite.config.ts , add the Tailwind plugin and the alias. Everything else stays as it is: In tsconfig.json , add this inside compilerOptions , so TypeScript understands the same shortcut: Create ClientApp/app.css with one line, and import it at the top of the client entry ( ClientApp/app.tsx for React, ClientApp/app.ts for Vue and Svelte): Now let shadcn set itself up and add the components we need. The flags answer its questions in advance (the nova preset is a clean neutral look); if you leave them out, it asks you instead. The Svelte tool asks before it changes app.css . Answer yes. Look in ClientApp/components/ui . Those files are yours now: open button and you will see ordinary code, not a library. When a library does almost what you want, you fight it. These are plain files in your repo. Want a rounder button? Edit the file. There is no version to upgrade and nothing hidden. Still, you rarely need to: theming (next) changes the look of every component at once. Make the theme yours Every shadcn component reads a few CSS variables, such as --primary for the main color. Add this to the end of ClientApp/app.css , and every button, switch and progress bar turns violet with rounder corners: Try other values to see how far one line goes. The .dark block is used when the page has the dark class on its root element; we do not add a switch here, but the theme is ready for one. The login page The template's login page is plain HTML, and Tailwind resets plain HTML to nothing. Replace it with a card. A Field groups a label, an input and its error message, so the error appears in the right place and is announced to screen readers. The form still uses withPrecognition : when you leave a field, the server checks it with the same rules as the real submit. Open http://localhost:5180/login to see the new look. 3. Add a database Lists and items must survive a restart, so they need a database. We use EF Core with SQLite : EF Core is the usual way to talk to a database from C , and SQLite needs no server. Use --version "11. " for the SQLite package. The EF Core version must match your .NET version. Create Data.cs . These classes are the database shape . They are not what the browser sees; that comes next. A few choices are worth explaining: - OwnerEmail instead of a users table. The template's demo user already has an email in the sign-in cookie. Using it as the owner key keeps this guide short. In a real app you would use ASP.NET Core Identity and a user id. - ShareSlug is null until you share. A random secret in the URL is the only thing that opens a public list. There is nothing to guess, and turning sharing off simply forgets the secret. - RemindedAt makes reminders safe to repeat. If the app restarts halfway through, a reminder that was already sent is never sent twice. - DateTime , not DateTimeOffset , for reminders. SQLite cannot compare DateTimeOffset values inside a query. We store UTC times as plain DateTime , and the query RemindAt () line - the /todos endpoints (the ones named todos.index , todos.store , todos.toggle and todos.destroy ) - the /dashboard endpoint and the DashboardPage record - the Todo , TodoStats , TodosPage , NewTodo and TodoStore types - their lines in AppJsonContext at the bottom Then register the database where the other services are registered: And create the tables right after var app = builder.Build(); : Production and tests need a different database than your laptop. With GetConnectionString("Default") they can set ConnectionStrings:Default without touching the code. We use this in the tests. EnsureCreated() builds the tables on the first run. It cannot change them later. When the model changes in a real app, switch to EF Core migrations. 4. Decide what the browser sees Never send a database entity to the browser. It may have columns you did not mean to share (like OwnerEmail ), and every change to the table would change your page. Send small records that hold only what a page needs. Create Models.cs : Three things here are easy to miss: - Form classes are public . The validation generator, AddValidation() , skips internal types. A private form class means the [Required] rules silently do nothing. - Events.RemindersChanged(email) is one value used twice. The page uses it to say "refresh me when this happens", and the worker uses it to say "this happened". Because both use the same value, they cannot drift apart. - Email() hides one claim lookup. Every endpoint asks the same question, "whose list is this?", so we ask it in one place. The template turned off reflection-based JSON, which keeps the app ready for Native AOT. The price is that you list every type that goes to or from the browser. Add these lines to AppJsonContext at the bottom of Program.cs : Each page record gets its own line when you create it: ListsPage in step 5, ListPage in step 6 and PublicPage in step 7. You get an error the first time that type is sent, and the message names the type. Add it and try again. 5. The lists page A page record holds the props of a page and also the code that fills them. Create ListsPage.cs : Add [JsonSerializable(typeof(ListsPage))] to AppJsonContext , then read the handler from top to bottom: 1. lists is read straight from the database into ListCard records. AsNoTracking() tells EF Core we will not change these rows, which makes the query cheaper. 2. Stats is deferred . The page is sent right away and the browser asks for the numbers a moment later. The visitor sees the page sooner, even if counting is slow. 3. .Cache(...) keeps the finished stats for five minutes, so a second visit does not count again. The tags give us a way to throw them away: every write will remove the tag user:email , so the numbers are never wrong for long. 4. Reminders is deferred and live . We come back to it in step 8. Now the routes. Create Endpoints.cs : Call it from Program.cs , in the place where the /dashboard endpoint used to be: Also send people to their lists after they sign in. In the /login endpoint, change the last "/dashboard" to "/lists" . .WithName("lists.store") costs nothing, and it pays you back twice. The name becomes routes.lists.store() in your frontend, so you never type "/lists" again. And the form's type, RouteBodies['lists.store'] , is taken from the C class NewList , so the C and the TypeScript cannot disagree. It does two jobs. A normal submit with bad data is sent back to the form with the error messages. And when the page asks, "is this one field valid?" while the person is still typing, the server answers without running your code. You write the rules once, on the class, with [Required] and [StringLength] . Make the frontend ready Write the types and routes files now. The app does this by itself when it starts in Development; this command does it on demand, which is handy in CI: Open ClientApp/types/routes.ts and look. You will find functions you did not write, one per named route: Now run the checker. It should fail, and that is the point: Because we deleted the todos and dashboard routes, TypeScript lists every place that still uses them: the layout and the home page. A string URL would have failed silently, in front of a visitor. A typed route fails at your desk. Fix them one by one. First the layout, which is used by every page. It has the top bar with the My lists link and the Log out button, and an Alert for the messages the server sends after an action (the flash messages): Then the home page, whose link pointed at the deleted todos route: Finally delete ClientApp/pages/Todos and the Dashboard page ( Dashboard.tsx , Dashboard.vue or Dashboard.svelte ). Run bun run build again. It passes. dotnet build prints INERTIA002 for ListsPage : "this component has no file under ClientApp/pages ". That is a helper catching a typo, or a page you forgot to write. It goes away in the next step, when we add the page. 6. One list, with infinite scroll A list can have thousands of items. Sending them all would make the page slow, so we send one page of items and the browser asks for the next page when the reader scrolls to the end. Create ListPage.cs , and add [JsonSerializable(typeof(ListPage))] to AppJsonContext : - .ToPageAsync(request) (from Inertia.Net.EntityFrameworkCore ) adds Skip and Take for you and counts the rows. PageRequest reads ?page=2 from the URL by itself. - The order must be unique. We sort by IsDone and then by Id . If two items could tie, a row might appear on two pages or on none. - Scroll(items) tells the browser that this value is a list that grows. New pages are merged into items.data instead of replacing it. - Someone else's list is a 404. The query asks for the id and the owner together. It does not reveal that the list exists. - links.GetPathByName("public.show", ...) is a named route used on the server . The page needs the public address, and the name builds it, so the URL pattern lives in one place only. (The route is added in step 7, until then the address is simply empty.) Add the rest of the routes inside MapForgetMeNot , after the two list routes. Add using System.Security.Cryptography; at the top of the file too: Notice the pattern. Each write checks the owner in the query , saves , clears the stats cache , and sends the person back with Back(...) . Back returns them to the page they came from, so the page shows the new state, and WithFlash carries the one-time message. GET /lists/5 is protected, but PATCH /items/9 is a separate door. Every endpoint that takes an id must check that the id belongs to the signed-in person. This is the most common security bug in apps like this one. Sharing works like this: the first press creates a random secret, and the second press forgets it. Eight random bytes are 16 characters nobody can guess. Do not use Random or a counter for a secret. Run bun run types again, so the browser knows the new routes and pages. Then add the two pages. The lists page. useForm holds the form's values, and withPrecognition gives it validate , which asks the server about one field: And the page for one list. Pay attention to InfiniteScroll : it wraps your rows and does the loading for you. Try it: 1. Open My lists and click Add with the box empty. The server answers with "The Title field is required". 2. Paste a title longer than 80 characters and click outside the box. The error appears before you submit. That is Precognition, and it is the same message the server would send. 3. Add a list, add a few items, tick one off and add a reminder. The numbers at the top change, because every write cleared the cached stats. - needs a fallback , even an empty one, or the page will not render. For the stats we show skeleton cards. For the reminders we show nothing until they arrive. - A change reloads the list from the first page. When you tick an item, the server sends the list again, so the extra pages you scrolled in are dropped. That is the price of the simple Back() redirect. If it matters for your app, reload only what changed with a partial reload. shadcn-svelte's Button is type="button" by default, so inside a form it does nothing. That is why the Svelte pages write type="submit" on their Add buttons. The React and Vue buttons submit by default. 7. Share a list, and render it on the server A shared list is a page that anyone can open, and many people may open the same one. That makes it the perfect page for server-side rendering (SSR) . Without SSR, the server sends an empty page and the browser has to download JavaScript, run it, and only then show the list. With SSR, the server runs your component first and sends finished HTML. Search engines and slow phones get the content at once, and the browser then "wakes up" the page with the same code. The share button already exists, from step 6. All that is missing is the page it points to. Create PublicPage.cs , add [JsonSerializable(typeof(PublicPage))] to AppJsonContext , and map the route: The page record: Look at the last line. .WithSsrCache(...) is the SSR cache . Rendering takes time, and this page looks the same for everyone, so the finished HTML can be reused: - For 5 minutes the saved HTML is served without calling the SSR server at all. - For one hour more it is still served, and a new render is made in the background ( staleFor ). Nobody waits. - The cache key is built from the page's JSON , which includes the title and the items. If the list changes, the JSON changes, the key changes, and the old render is never used. You cannot show a stale page by mistake. A page with per-person props makes one cache entry per person. That wastes memory and gains nothing. Our list pages are not cached for that reason, and the public page is. Turn SSR on. In AddInertia(...) in Program.cs , add: UseNodeProcess makes the app start and watch the SSR process for you. If it stops answering, it is restarted, and while it is down the pages are rendered in the browser instead. Use n.Executable = "node" if you do not have Bun. The SSR process listens on port 13714. If a second Inertia.Net app tries to start its own on the same machine, its SSR process cannot start, and that app quietly renders in the browser instead (you will see a warning in the log). Give each app its own port: o.Ssr.UseNodeProcess(n = { n.Executable = "bun"; n.BasePort = 13715; }) , and set the same port in the inertia({ ssr: { port: ... } }) line of vite.config.ts , then run the build again. The port is written into the SSR bundle when it is built, so changing only the C side does not work. We ran two apps side by side this way and both rendered on the server. The SSR bundle needs an entry file and a build setting. The entry is two lines: In vite.config.ts , tell the Inertia plugin where the entry is, and build the SSR bundle into the ssr folder with its dependencies included, so it runs without node modules : Change the build script in package.json so it builds both bundles: Use vue-tsc --noEmit (Vue) or svelte-check --tsconfig ./tsconfig.json (Svelte) instead of tsc --noEmit . The template's script already has the right one; only add the last part. And the public page: Code in a page runs in Node or Bun during SSR, where there is no window or document . That is why Show uses a relative link and not window.location.origin . If a component must use the browser, do it inside an effect, which runs only in the browser. To see it work, build, start the app in the Production setting, and look at the page source of a shared list. The list title and items are there as real HTML: While Vite runs in development, Vite does the rendering itself and the SSR cache is switched off, so every change shows at once. That is why you build and run in Production to see the real thing. 8. A reminder that appears by itself Add a reminder time to an item. When the time comes, the My lists page should show it, without anyone reloading. Two parts make that work: a worker that notices due reminders, and a live prop that refreshes the page when told. First the worker. A BackgroundService runs for as long as the app runs: - Every 20 seconds is plenty for a demo. A real app might use a minute. - CreateScope() gives the worker its own AppDb . The worker lives forever, but a database context must not. - Save first, publish second. The reminders are marked as sent before anyone is told. If the app dies in between, nobody gets the same reminder twice. - try / catch around the work. If one round fails, the worker logs it and tries again next time instead of stopping for good. Now the line that connects the worker to the page. In ListsPage we wrote .Live(Events.RemindersChanged(email)) . When the worker publishes that event, the browser reloads only the reminders prop. Nothing else on the page is touched. Install the SignalR transport. It carries the "something changed" message to the browser: In Program.cs , register it and the worker, and map the connection endpoint: Without it, nobody can join a private channel. With it, a person can join only the channel named after their own email. Without this check, anyone could listen to anyone's reminders. Keep the rule tight. Finally, turn the client side on. The template already includes ClientApp/lib/inertia-signalr.ts . Import it in the client entry ( app.tsx or app.ts ) and pass it to createInertiaApp : Run it. Add an item with a reminder one minute from now, open My lists and wait. When the time comes, the reminder shows up on its own. Open the browser's network tab to see how little happens: one small request, only for reminders . Polling asks "anything new?" every few seconds, for every open page, all day. A live prop sends nothing until something changes, and then sends one small request. It is cheaper for the server and faster for the person. A SignalR message reaches only the browsers connected to the server that sent it, and each server would also run its own worker. Behind a load balancer, add a Redis backplane, keep the props cache in Redis (see Redis cache), and run the worker on one instance. For a single server, what you have now is right. 9. Test the important paths You have a few rules the app must never break: nobody reads another person's list, a private list has no public page, and the dashboard's slow numbers arrive after the page. Tests make sure these stay true. Create a test project next to the app. Make sure its TargetFramework matches the app's: The test project starts your real app in memory, so add one line at the very end of Program.cs of the app: Delete the generated UnitTest1.cs and create ListTests.cs : Read the setup, because it explains most of the rest: - A fresh database file per test class. Tests must not see each other's lists. - o.Version = "test" fixes the asset version, so requests do not need a first visit to learn it. - SsrMode.Disabled means no Bun is started during tests. - AllowAutoRedirect = false lets a test look at the redirect itself, such as "a signed-out visitor is sent to /login ". - HandleCookies = true keeps the sign-in cookie and the anti-forgery cookie between requests, like a browser. Run them: The template protects every form against CSRF. A real browser gets a cookie and sends it back as a header. In a test, WithXsrfToken copies the token from a page response into your request, so the server accepts it. If a test fails with a 400, this is usually the reason. 10. Run it in production Build both bundles and publish: Before the app is public, go through this short list. Each item has a reason. Do this Why --- --- Install Bun (or set Executable = "node" ) where the app runs The app starts the SSR bundle with it Keep the Data Protection keys somewhere that survives a restart The sign-in cookie is encrypted with them. A new key signs everyone out Use EF Core migrations instead of EnsureCreated() The tables will change, and EnsureCreated() cannot change them Set ConnectionStrings Default for the real database The file next to the app is only for your laptop Forward the proxy headers when you run behind one The sign-in rate limit counts clients by address, and every client looks like the proxy. See Deploying behind a proxy Run one instance, or add Redis for the caches and SignalR The props cache, SSR cache and live messages are per server unless you share them Container examples are in Deploying behind a proxy and the server-side rendering guide. For the container's memory, use the memory table. If something does not build Compare your Program.cs with the finished one: Where to go next You used page records, named and typed routes, Precognition, deferred and cached props, ToPageAsync , infinite scroll, server-side rendering with its cache, live props and the testing helpers. These are the next ones to try: - Once props: remember a value that never changes on the client, such as a list of countries. - Merging props and Partial reloads: update part of a page without replacing it. - Redis cache: share the props and SSR caches between servers. - Authentication: replace the demo user with ASP.NET Core Identity. - Native AOT: a much smaller and faster-starting app, once you avoid EF Core. - Performance: what each feature costs, measured.

title: Quick start
description: Add Inertia.Net to an ASP.NET Core app, create the root template and render your first page.
body: Already using the starter template? Its services, middleware, root template and frontend are configured for you. These steps are for adding Inertia to an existing app or building one manually. Every app needs the same four things: 1. Register the services Choose one backend style. All three use the same protocol middleware and the same Render(...) result. AddValidation() enables the Minimal API integration used by .WithInertiaValidation() . UseInertiaAntiforgery() issues the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and validates every unsafe request, so forms work from the first commit. See Precognition for live form validation. 2. Add the root template The root template is an HTML file in the content root. The default name is app.html . For Vue and Svelte, remove @viteReactRefresh and point @vite at ClientApp/app.ts . @inertia is required. The other tokens are described in Pages and responses. Make sure app.html is copied to the output and publish directory: 3. Create the page component The page name passed to Render must match the client resolver. With @inertiajs/vite the resolver maps ClientApp/pages/ automatically. The client entry only needs to start Inertia: Pass your own resolve and setup functions to createInertiaApp . The client setup page shows both forms for React, Vue and Svelte. 4. Run it Install dependencies and start Vite from the project directory with your package manager: Package manager Install dependencies Start Vite Build assets --- --- --- --- npm npm install npm run dev npm run build Bun bun install bun run dev bun run build pnpm pnpm install pnpm run dev pnpm run build Yarn yarn install yarn run dev yarn run build Keep Vite running in terminal 1. Start ASP.NET Core in terminal 2: Open the URL printed by dotnet watch (not the Vite URL). The first visit to / should display “Hello from .NET”. For production, run the build command from your row, then publish the app: Deploy wwwroot/build and app.html with the published app. Where to go next Vite configuration and the React, Vue and Svelte entries. Lazy, deferred, merged and cached page data. Redirects, error bags and Precognition. Render the first visit on Node.

title: Client setup
description: Configure Vite and the React, Vue or Svelte client for an Inertia.Net app.
body: Inertia.Net speaks the Inertia.js v3 protocol. Install a v3 client package; v2 clients are not supported. Install the client Run client setup commands from the ASP.NET Core project directory (the one containing your .csproj ). npm, Bun, pnpm and Yarn are supported. The framework snippets use npm spelling; replace the command with the equivalent for your package manager: Package manager Add packages Add development packages --- --- --- npm npm install npm install -D Bun bun add bun add -D pnpm pnpm add pnpm add -D Yarn yarn add yarn add -D Replace with the names and version ranges from your framework's snippet. If the project has no package.json , create one first with npm init -y , bun init -y , pnpm init or yarn init . @types/node types the node:fs import and process in the Vite config. Add vite/client to tsconfig.json so import.meta.glob is typed: Use "jsx": "preserve" or omit it for Vue and Svelte. The starter templates use ClientApp/pages . The manual examples below use resources/js/Pages . Keep the resolver, file paths and Vite entry consistent with the layout you choose. The templates also ship ClientApp/lib/inertia-signalr.ts , the client transport for live props over SignalR. Uncomment live: signalr() in ClientApp/app.tsx (or app.ts ) to turn it on. Vite configuration The Vite config is the same for every client except the framework plugin and the entry file ( app.tsx for React, app.ts for Vue and Svelte). Add these fields to package.json : The manifest key of the entry ( resources/js/app.tsx for React, resources/js/app.ts for Vue and Svelte) is what you pass to @vite("...") . Client entry The optional @inertiajs/vite plugin resolves pages and mounts the app for you. With it, the entry is just: Without the plugin, provide the resolver and setup yourself. Pages A page file receives the props from Render(...) as normal component props. Inertia.Net can write TypeScript declarations for your page props, shared props and flash data. See TypeScript types. Development workflow Open the ASP.NET Core URL, not the Vite URL. Two servers run side by side: URL What it is Open it? --- --- --- http://localhost:5180 (the template's default) Your app. ASP.NET Core routes the request, runs your endpoint and renders the Inertia page. Yes http://localhost:5173 The Vite dev server. It only serves JavaScript, CSS and hot-reload updates to the page above. No. It has no pages, so it shows a blank page. Vite prints localhost:5173 prominently when it starts, but that address is for the browser's asset requests, not for you. In Development the app reads wwwroot/hot and renders the Vite tags; in production it reads the manifest. For production: Node is needed to build the assets and only needed at runtime when SSR is enabled. Using @inertiajs/vite The plugin also contributes the SSR dev endpoint and page resolution. Add it before the hot-file plugin: Keep the SSR listener on loopback: the renderer trusts its output and has no authentication. The SSR guide covers the full setup.

title: Precognition
description: Validate a form before submission without running its handler.
body: The Minimal API React sample includes a login validation demo. It accepts dummy values and does not create an authentication session. Precognition sends the same POST as the form with Precognition: true . The server validates it and returns without running the handler: The message is the first returned error. A valid request returns 204 and Precognition-Success: true . For Minimal APIs register AddValidation() and use: The sample's input model is: Import System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations . This replaces .WithInertiaValidation() ; do not use both. It also handles normal validation redirects. Filters added after it do not run on precognitive requests. FastEndpoints enables this through c.ConfigureInertia() ; MVC does not support Precognition. Client setup Inertia 3 includes Precognition in its form integration. Each example validates on blur and displays the error: Precognition-Validate-Only selects returned errors by field, including nested paths. Validation still runs the validator: keep database rules cheap. Validate on blur for login and payment forms to avoid an error while the user is still typing. setValidationTimeout(3000) raises the debounce interval for expensive rules; it is not the HTTP deadline. Antiforgery and authorization UseInertiaAntiforgery() validates precognitive POSTs like other unsafe requests; the Inertia client sends the token automatically. Authorization middleware runs before endpoint filters, so protected forms validate only for authorized users. Rate limiting Precognitive POSTs pass through rate limiting before the endpoint filter, so using a single strict login bucket can lock users out while typing. Use separate bounded partitions for validation and real submissions, and check endpoint InertiaPrecognitionMetadata as well as InertiaPrecognition.IsPrecognitive(request) : the header alone does not guarantee the handler is skipped. Do not use GetNoLimiter for validation; validators consume CPU and may query a database. With the metadata present the handler is skipped, so the validation bucket does not allow credential attempts. On a rejected precognitive request set Precognition: true on the 429 response. This lets the client recognize the response; the validation request still rejects, so provide a retry or error message. Run UseRouting , UseRateLimiter , UseInertia and UseInertiaAntiforgery in that order. See the example below for a complete policy. The following AddServices method is copied from the Minimal API sample's LoginDemo class. The sample's generation field exists only to reset E2E test buckets; real apps can partition on a stable client identity appropriate to their deployment. Import System.Globalization , System.Threading.RateLimiting and Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting , and declare private static int generation; and private static int submissions; in that class. The complete sample class includes LoginForm , LoginPage , and the reset helper: Register it before building the app. The sample also opts 429 into error-page handling for real Inertia submissions; 429 is not a default error-page status: Map an error page with a retry message. Precognitive requests accepting JSON retain their 429 response and Precognition: true header. Attach the policy to the endpoint: The sample routes use this method: The sample partitions by remote IP for demonstration; configure trusted forwarded headers when behind a proxy and choose a partition key suited to your authentication and abuse model. Testing With an Inertia.Net.Testing client that retains cookies, load the form page and attach its XSRF token. For an endpoint that validates email : Import System.Net , System.Net.Http.Json , System.Text.Json , Inertia.Net and Inertia.Net.Testing . Testing shows the client and token setup. Protocol reference Header Direction Meaning --- --- --- Precognition: true Request and response Identifies a validation request and response Precognition-Validate-Only Request Comma-separated client field paths whose errors are returned Precognition-Success: true Response Validation succeeded (204) Vary: Precognition Response Varies the response by request type A validation failure returns 422 ; a limiter may return 429 . InertiaPrecognition.IsPrecognitive(HttpRequest) checks the header; InertiaPrecognitionMetadata identifies endpoints whose handler is skipped for these requests.

title: AI agents
description: Give coding agents the context and conventions they need to build Inertia.Net pages correctly.
headings: Point the agent at the docs
Let the agent check its own work
body: An Inertia.Net app is a good fit for coding agents. The backend and the frontend live in one project, a feature follows one request path (endpoint, props, page component), and there is no API contract or client router for the agent to keep in sync. The main thing an agent needs is to know the conventions. This page gives you that context in a form you can paste into your project. Point the agent at the docs The documentation is published as plain text for language models: URL Contents --- --- /llms.txt An index of every page with a one-line summary, following the llms.txt format. /llms-full.txt The whole documentation in one Markdown file. Agents that can fetch URLs can read these directly. For agents that cannot, download llms-full.txt into your repository (for example as docs/inertia-net.md ) and reference it from your agent instructions. Add an AGENTS.md section Most coding agents read a project instruction file: AGENTS.md for Codex and many others, CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, .github/copilot-instructions.md for GitHub Copilot and .cursor/rules for Cursor. Copy this section into yours and adjust the paths and framework to match your app. If you use Vue or Svelte, change the component path and extension. Asking for a feature Agents do better with a request that names both ends of the feature. For example: Add a /projects page. The endpoint returns Projects/Index with a paginated projects prop using Merge and the InfiniteScroll component, and a deferred stats prop. Add a create form that posts to /projects , validates CreateProjectInput with .WithInertiaValidation() , and redirects back with a toast flash message. Add a test with Inertia.Net.Testing for the page component and props. A request like this tells the agent which props to use, how validation is wired, and how to check the result with testing helpers. Let the agent check its own work Agents are most reliable when they can verify a change. Inertia.Net gives them a few cheap checks: - Compile-time types. With generated TypeScript types, a prop renamed in C breaks the client build, so the client build script ( npm run build , bun run build , pnpm run build or yarn run build ) catches mismatches. - Response tests. Inertia.Net.Testing asserts the component name and props without a browser. Ask the agent to add one test per page. - Missing components. In Development, DevTools checks report a Render call whose page component does not exist. dotnet new inertia -n MyApp --framework react creates an app with pages, a validated form, flash messages, CSRF and Vite already set up. Starting an agent from the template gives it working examples of every convention above.

title: DevTools
description: Record visits for the Inertia DevTools extension and catch missing page components during development.
body: The Inertia DevTools browser extension shows every visit, its props, headers and page state. Inertia.Net implements the server protocol. Enable DevTools Each request through UseInertia() gets an X-Inertia-Devtools-Id and an entry in memory (per browser tab, at most MaxEntriesPerTab and MaxEntries , for MaxAge ): request type, timings, headers, bodies, the page object and its props metadata. The first page carries the discovery tag the extension reads. Values of names containing password , secret , token , authorization , cookie or api key are replaced with [REDACTED] in props, bodies and headers. Add names with RedactedKeys . Nothing leaves the app. Sensitive query parameters are also redacted in recorded request/page URLs, redirects and URL headers; actual application URLs are unchanged. Malformed JSON bodies are omitted. Only eligible Inertia text bodies with a known length up to MaxBodyBytes are buffered; unknown-length nonseekable bodies are omitted as streamed, so recording does not spool bulk requests to disk. Outside Development nothing is recorded unless Enabled = true , and the read API answers only requests that Authorize accepts ( 404 otherwise). With Pages.Directory set, entries link the component to its file. Page component check In Development, Render throws when the component has no page file, naming the closest one: Names match exactly, as the client resolver does, even on case-insensitive file systems. Outside Development there is no check and no file access. Pages.Extensions lists the file types: .tsx , .jsx , .ts , .js , .vue and .svelte by default. Generated TypeScript The development startup also writes TypeScript declarations when o.TypeScript.OutputPath is set. It only writes the file when the content changed. See TypeScript types. What to check before deploying - Pages.Directory can stay configured; it is inactive outside Development. - DevTools recording is off unless explicitly enabled. - The generated TypeScript file is committed if the client build type-checks in CI. - Production logs do not contain the DevTools read API. Install the Inertia DevTools extension, open your app in Development, and use the extension's panel. The server entries are correlated by the X-Inertia-Devtools-Id header. Without an Authorize callback, the read API responds only in Development. Requests must come from this machine through a loopback connection to a loopback host name such as localhost . They must have no X-Forwarded-For , Forwarded , X-Forwarded-Host , X-Real-IP or Via header. Set Authorize to allow access from a container or another machine. A reverse proxy on the same machine makes remote requests look local if it adds none of those headers. Set Authorize in that case too. If recording is enabled outside Development without an Authorize callback, the app logs a warning and the read API returns 404. Map the read API with MapInertiaDevTools() and authorize its users. The recorder's process-wide latch stays active after first use. The process-wide latch for parallel-prop planning does too.

title: First 10 minutes
description: Start a template app, try its validated form, and test the redirect.
body: Create the React starter (choose vue or svelte for another client; add --tfm net11.0 to target .NET 11 instead of .NET 10): Use bun install and bun run dev , pnpm install and pnpm run dev , or yarn install and yarn run dev if you prefer. In a second terminal run dotnet run . Open the address printed by dotnet run ( http://localhost:5180 for the template) and visit /todos ; submit an empty title to see the validation message. The template includes Vite, antiforgery and a complete form. Vite prints http://localhost:5173 when it starts, but that server only supplies JavaScript, CSS and hot reload to your app. It has no pages, so opening it shows a blank page. Your app is the ASP.NET Core address from dotnet run : http://localhost:5180 . The handler in Program.cs is: NewTodo.Title has [Required, StringLength(100)] ; invalid requests redirect with errors before the handler runs. The template's ClientApp/pages/Todos/Index.tsx ( Index.vue or Index.svelte for the other clients) uses useForm to submit and display the error: To test the round trip, add Inertia.Net.Testing and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing to a test project, expose public partial class Program; in the app, and create a cookie-preserving WebApplicationFactory client with AllowAutoRedirect = false : See Testing for named error bags and custom XSRF names, and Quick start for an existing application.

title: Vite
description: Manifest tags, the dev-server hot file, asset base URLs, prefetching and CSP nonces.
body: ViteAssets (a singleton, also usable directly as vite.RenderTags(httpContext, "resources/js/app.tsx") ) renders the tags for the @vite(...) token and the tag helper. Production In production Inertia.Net reads wwwroot/build/.vite/manifest.json (falling back to wwwroot/build/manifest.json for older Vite). It parses the manifest once and pre-renders the tags to UTF-8. For each entry it emits, in order: 1. for the entry's CSS and the CSS of its static imports, recursively and deduplicated; 2. for the entry file; 3. for each static import. URLs are {PathBase}/{BuildDirectory}/{file} so apps under a path base work, or {AssetBaseUrl}/{file} . An entry missing from the manifest throws with the list of available entries. A missing manifest throws with the paths it looked in. Development While the dev server runs, the tags are @vite/client and the entry from the dev server origin, plus the React Refresh preamble for @viteReactRefresh . The dev server counts as running when: - o.Vite.DevServerUrl is set (always, in any environment), or - the environment is Development and the hot file ( wwwroot/hot by default) exists and contains the origin. The hot file is written by your Vite config. The @inertiajs/vite plugin does not write one, so the samples include a small plugin that does. Built assets are served from /build/ , so the Vite base is /build/ for a build. The dev server must serve from the root because Inertia.Net emits {origin}/@vite/client and {origin}/{entry} . Use base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/' . Options Only plain http(s) origins without quotes or markup are accepted from the hot file or DevServerUrl , because the origin is echoed into a script. With AssetBaseUrl set, Vite's own base must match so lazily imported chunks resolve against the CDN too: Prefetching Page components resolved with lazy import.meta.glob are separate chunks that the browser downloads only when a page needs them. o.Vite.Prefetch downloads them after the page loads, at low priority, so the next navigation does not wait: The tags get one small inline script with the list of chunks the entries can import later (dynamic imports, then their static imports and CSS), minus those already loaded. It is rendered once per entry set. Content Security Policy With a nonce-based CSP, set o.CspNonce to the request's nonce. Every script and stylesheet tag Inertia.Net writes then carries it: the page , the Vite tags, the React refresh preamble and the prefetch script (whose links get it too). The nonce must be base64 or base64url; anything else throws. Cached tags are split where the nonce goes, so a nonce costs one copy of the tag bytes per request and no re-rendering. Use app.UseStaticFiles() with a long Cache-Control for /build/assets , or app.MapStaticAssets() when the client is built before dotnet publish . See Deploying.

title: Props
description: Lazy, optional, deferred, merged, once, cached and rescued page data.
body: Props are the data a page receives. Render(component, props) takes an InertiaProps , a string-keyed dictionary, or a typed object. Nested InertiaProps and dictionaries are walked, so props can be nested at any depth. Every page has an errors prop. Its key order is errors , shared props, then page props. C 15 unions (.NET 11). A prop whose type is a union (for example public union Subject(User, Team); ) is written as the JSON of its active case, with no wrapper or discriminator, through your source-generated JsonSerializerContext ; partial reloads select it like any other prop. An InertiaProp ( Defer , Optional , ...) stored inside a union case is not resolved: keep lazy props at the page level. The prop factories C\ Behavior --- --- ["title"] = "Hi" A plain value. Sent on every response that includes the key. Prop(() = ...) Lazy: the loader runs only when the prop is part of the response. Always(value) or Always(() = ...) Sent even when a partial reload does not ask for it. Optional(() = ...) Never sent on the first visit, only when a partial reload asks for it. Defer(() = ..., group: "name") Left out of the first response. The client loads it right away with its group. Merge(value) The client appends the new value to its current one. DeepMerge(value) The client deep merges the value. Once(() = ...) Resolved once and remembered by the client. Scroll(page, wrapper: "data", metadata) An infinite-scroll prop with paging metadata. Every lazy factory ( Prop , Always , Optional , Defer , Merge , DeepMerge , Once , Scroll ) accepts five loader shapes: The token is HttpContext.RequestAborted . An async lambda always binds to the awaiting overload, never to “a prop whose value is a Task”. Fluent methods mutate and return the same instance: .Once(key?, until?) , .As(key) , .Until(ttl) , .Fresh() , .Append(path?, matchOn?) , .Prepend(path?, matchOn?) , .DeepMerge() , .MatchOn(params keys) , .Defer(group) , .WithGroup(group) , .Rescue() , .Parallel() , .Cache(key, duration) and .Cache(key, duration, staleFor?, tags?) . Fresh() makes a prop a once prop, and WithGroup() makes it deferred. Repeated MatchOn() calls add keys. Root Append() and Prepend() are mutually exclusive and combining them throws. Fluent methods mutate the prop, so create prop instances per request; do not share them across requests. Resolution order Loaders run sequentially by default, in prop order, and only when their prop is included in the response. That makes a scoped EF Core DbContext safe to use in several loaders. The page is buffered before it is sent, so a loader that throws never produces a half-written 200 . Parallel props Mark independent async loaders with .Parallel() to start them together: - Only Task and ValueTask loaders can be parallel. Parallel() throws for values and synchronous loaders. - At most InertiaOptions.Props.MaxConcurrency loaders run at once per render (default 4). - Top-level props and props inside literal objects ( InertiaProps and other string-keyed dictionaries) start early. Elsewhere they resolve in turn. - Loaders of props that are not part of the response never start. - If a loader fails, the others are cancelled and awaited, and the render fails with the first failure in prop order. A Rescue() d prop fails alone. A parallel loader must not use the request's DbContext or other non-thread-safe scoped services, and must not touch HttpContext . Give each loader its own context through IDbContextFactory or its own scope. Scoped services in loaders Prop (...) hands a loader a service from the request, without capturing it in a closure: - A loader that runs during the request gets the request's instance (the same DbContext the handler used). - A .Parallel() loader gets a scope of its own, so two parallel loaders never share a DbContext . The scope is disposed when the loader finishes. - A stale-while-revalidate refresh runs after the response, in a new scope disposed when the refresh ends. - A service that is not registered fails the render with the prop's path and the service type. Deferred props Defer leaves the prop out of the first response and lists it under deferredProps . The client asks for each group as soon as the page is mounted. See Deferred props for the client component and the request rules. Merge props The full behavior is in Merging props. Once props When the client already holds the key it sends X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props ; the value is left out while the onceProps entry stays. See Once props. Cached props .Cache(key, duration) keeps a prop's value as JSON in the cache (the app's IMemoryCache by default). A hit costs neither the query nor serialization. Every request that uses a key gets the same value. Put the user, tenant or anything else the value depends on in the key. Keys live in their own cache space and cannot collide with the app's own entries. Only loading changes: optional, deferred, merged, once and scroll props keep their behavior, and their metadata is written from the cache too. A parallel cached prop does not start its loader on a hit. A rescued failure is not cached. Removing and replacing values. Inject IInertiaCache where the data changes: ClearPropsAsync() removes every cached prop and ClearSsrAsync() every cached render. SetPropAsync serializes the value as a prop of its type would, and takes the same staleFor and tags . Stale-while-revalidate. staleFor keeps serving a value after its duration. The first request that reads a stale value gets it at once, and the loader runs after the response has been sent. Past duration + staleFor the loader runs during the request again. - Response completion enqueues refreshes on a bounded background worker; it does not wait for the loader. Loaders using staleFor must use singleton dependencies or create an independent scope inside the loader with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope() or IDbContextFactory . Do not capture request-scoped services or HttpContext . - The worker accepts 64 pending refreshes, runs up to 4 at a time, cancels each one after 30 seconds and cancels them all on host shutdown. A full queue drops the refresh and logs a warning, leaving the stale value at its existing expiration. Monitor inertia.cache.refresh.dropped , tagged with inertia.cache.kind=prop ssr . - One refresh runs per key and app instance at a time. A refresh that finds the value fresh again skips its loader. - A fill or refresh whose loader started before an IInertiaCache removal ( RemovePropAsync , RemoveByTagAsync , ClearPropsAsync ) on the same app instance does not store its value; the request still gets it. - A refresh that fails is logged as a warning and keeps the stale value; the next stale read tries again. Another store. Props and SSR renders live in an IInertiaCacheStore . Register your own singleton before or after AddInertia() : The store gets and sets byte arrays by InertiaCacheKey , removes by key and by tag, and reads unknown formats as a miss. While a page renders, a store that throws is logged (at most once every 30 seconds) and counts as a miss; IInertiaCache lets the exception through. For a store shared by every app instance, Inertia.Net.Redis registers one with AddInertiaRedisCache(...) . See Redis cache. Typed page props A typed object is AOT-friendly: it is walked through its JsonTypeInfo , and members of type InertiaProp are resolved by Inertia.Net while the rest is serialized normally. Register UsersPage and its value types in your JsonSerializerContext under Native AOT. Anonymous types work only when reflection-based serialization is enabled, so not under AOT. Dot keys Cached props under dot keys use the cache too. A top-level key containing dots is unpacked. ["user.name"] = "Ann" becomes "user": { "name": "Ann" } . BigInteger safety With o.PreserveBigIntegers = true , integers beyond ±(2^53 − 1) are written as {"$bigint":"9007199254740993"} and the page gets "preserveBigIntegers": true . Rescue .Rescue() keeps a page alive when one prop fails: If the loader throws, the exception is logged, the prop is left out of props , and its path goes to "rescuedProps": ["recommendations"] . Without .Rescue() the exception propagates normally. Cancellation of the request is never rescued.

title: Multiple apps and libraries
description: Mount a second Inertia UI under its own path, with its own shared props, asset version, state cookie, root view, error pages and SSR.
headings: What a mount keeps to itself
A root view shipped by a library
body: One ASP.NET Core app can serve more than one Inertia UI. A typical case is a library, such as an admin dashboard, that ships its own prebuilt client and is mounted under /dashboard in a host app that already uses Inertia.Net. Each UI is a mount : a named InertiaOptions that app.UseInertia(name) selects inside an app.Map(...) branch. The default mount is the one AddInertia(...) and UseInertia() configure, so existing apps do not change. What a mount keeps to itself Per mount Shared by all mounts --- --- Shared props ( o.Share ) and every other InertiaOptions setting IInertiaCache and the cache store (choose distinct InertiaProp.Cache(key) keys) Asset version: the 409 check only compares against the mount's own version IInertiaLive and the SignalR hub State cookie: .Inertia.State.{name} and .Inertia.Previous.{name} by default Metrics (named mounts add an inertia.mount tag) and DevTools Root view: the mount's RootView file, or a keyed IInertiaRootView Antiforgery and data protection Vite manifest, SSR servers, managed Node processes, TypeScript output The SSR HttpClient (its ConnectTimeout comes from the default mount) Error pages registered with AddInertiaErrorPages(name, ...) Register and map a mount Map sets the request's path base, so page URLs, Back() fallbacks, Vite asset URLs and the previous-URL cookie stay inside /dashboard . Calling AddInertia("dashboard", ...) again adds to that mount's configuration. Startup fails when UseInertia(name) names a mount that was never registered, or when two mounts share a state or previous-URL cookie name. A root view shipped by a library A library cannot rely on a file in the host's content root. Register a keyed IInertiaRootView that writes an embedded template instead: Error pages per mount A mount renders only the error components registered for it, because another mount's components are not in its bundle. A mount without AddInertiaErrorPages(name, ...) leaves its errors to the rest of the pipeline. SSR, health checks and TypeScript Each mount has its own SSR gateway, and its own managed Node processes when o.Ssr.UseNodeProcess() is set; give each mount its own BasePort . Check a mount's SSR servers with: o.TypeScript.OutputPath is per mount too, so each client gets its own generated declarations. For library authors Expose one registration call and one mapping call, and keep the mount name private to the library: Mounts are adapter configuration: the Inertia protocol on the wire does not change.

title: Live props
description: Props that refresh themselves when the server broadcasts an event.
body: A live prop refreshes itself when the server broadcasts an event. The page response says which props listen to which events; the client subscribes to those channels and, when an event arrives, reloads the affected props or applies the values the event carries. Components never subscribe or clean up. Three pieces make it work: 1. An event , defined once as a LiveEvent and shared by both sides. 2. A prop marked .Live(event) , which puts its listeners in the page's liveProps . 3. A publish through IInertiaLive , delivered to subscribers by a transport. Live props need @inertiajs/react , @inertiajs/vue3 or @inertiajs/svelte 3.11.0 or later. Older clients ignore liveProps . Define each event once A LiveEvent is an event name on a LiveChannel . The same value declares the prop and publishes the event, so the two sides cannot drift apart. Channels are LiveChannel.Public , Private , Presence or EncryptedPrivate . Names carry no prefix; a transport adds private- or presence- itself when its protocol needs one. Mark props live The page lists every listener, including those of props it left out: Call Effect --- --- .Live(event) Adds a listener. Repeatable: call it once per event. .Live(channel, "Created", "Deleted") Listens to several events on one channel. Live(() = ..., event) The factory form of Prop(...).Live(event) . .Throttle(window) The shortest time between two reloads of the prop. The client's default is one second. What combines with live Prop Live? Notes --- --- --- Prop , Always , shared props Yes Defer , Optional Yes Listeners are reported even while the value is left out. Once Yes A once prop the client already holds stays subscribed. Rescue , Parallel Yes A rescued prop stays subscribed; the next event fetches it again. Cache Yes Publishing does not evict the cache. Remove the entry with IInertiaCache first. Merge , DeepMerge , Scroll No A live prop is replaced whole, so these throw InvalidOperationException . Reload them from the page instead: see Reloading scroll and merge props. A live prop inside an array reloads its whole array, as every partial reload of an array descendant does. Prefer keyed objects for lists that change often. Shared live props A shared live prop keeps something current on every page, such as a notification bell: Publish events AddInertiaLive() registers IInertiaLive . A transport registers the IInertiaLiveBroadcaster that delivers what it publishes. - Without values , every client reloads the live props that listen to the event, each with its own request and its own data. - With values , keyed by prop path ( "auth.user" stays a flat key), those props are updated in place. Values use the page serializer options, so they match what a reload returns; under Native AOT the type needs to be in your registered JSON context, like any prop type. - exceptSocketId leaves one connection out, usually the client that made the change. The client sends its id as X-Socket-Id and HttpContext.InertiaRequest().SocketId reads it. The header is client-supplied, so it is only ever used to exclude. A broadcast reaches every client on the channel. Only publish values that everyone allowed on the channel may see. When a value depends on the user, publish without values and let each client reload its own. What a broadcaster delivers: On the client Read a live prop like any other prop. useProp exposes its loading state, and the cancelable live router event can hold an update back, for example to show a "new posts" button instead: SignalR Inertia.Net.Live.SignalR runs the transport inside your app: a SignalR hub the browser subscribes to, channel authorization, and the broadcaster that IInertiaLive publishes through. Apps created with dotnet new inertia ship the client transport as ClientApp/lib/inertia-signalr.ts . In other apps, copy the file in, then turn it on: @microsoft/signalr loads on the first subscription, so pages without live props never download it. When a dropped connection comes back, the transport joins its channels again and Inertia reloads every live prop once, catching up on missed events. Who may join a channel Channel Who joins --- --- Public Anyone who reaches the hub. Set o.AuthorizePublicChannels = true to ask the authorizer too. Private , Presence , EncryptedPrivate Only connections the authorizer allows. With no authorizer, nobody. For rules that need services, implement ILiveChannelAuthorizer and register it with o.Authorize () . It is created for each subscription, with constructor injection. SignalR has no presence member lists or end-to-end encryption, so presence and encrypted-private channels are authorized like private ones. The hub answers requests from other origins with 403 (add trusted ones to o.AllowedOrigins ). That check stands in for antiforgery tokens on the hub. Connections close when their authentication expires. SignalR groups live on one server. Behind several instances, add a Redis backplane ( AddSignalR().AddStackExchangeRedis(...) ) or Azure SignalR Service; without one, a publish reaches only the clients connected to the instance that sent it. The package README lists the client options, how channels map to SignalR groups, and the security notes. Reloading scroll and merge props A Scroll(...) or Merge(...) prop cannot be live: a live reload would merge the reloaded page into the list. Reload it from the page instead, with ClientApp/lib/inertia-live-reload.ts (in dotnet new inertia apps): Events within debounce milliseconds (default 250) become one reload, a reload waits for a visit in flight, the scroll position is kept, and the client that caused the event ( exceptSocketId ) is not reloaded. reset replaces the prop instead of merging it, so the reload brings no duplicates. The SignalR client transport delivers a channel's events to every subscriber. See Typed routes for routes.ts . Custom transports The page metadata and the payload do not depend on SignalR, so any transport works: - Pusher-protocol servers (Reverb, Soketi, Ably, Pusher) work with the client's built-in pusher() or echo() transport. On the server, implement IInertiaLiveBroadcaster with your server's publish API. - Anything else (Action Cable, server-sent events, Azure Web PubSub): implement IInertiaLiveBroadcaster on the server and a LiveTransport on the client. A broadcaster has one method. It receives the channel, the finished payload and the connection to skip: Testing InertiaPage.LiveProps holds the metadata, and HasLive asserts it, with the channel written as "{type}:{name}" : Limits, proxies and authorization changes SignalR defaults to 64 subscriptions per connection and a 200-character channel name. Configure MaxSubscriptionsPerConnection and MaxChannelNameLength through the SignalR options; both must be positive. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy configure trusted forwarded headers once and run UseForwardedHeaders() before the hub so origin and scheme checks see the external address. Authorization is checked when a client subscribes, not continuously. If access changes, disconnect the client or use a transport/application strategy that enforces revocation. A removed event can tell the UI to update, but it is not a security revocation mechanism.

title: Merging props
description: Append, prepend, deep merge and match items instead of replacing the client's value.
body: By default a reloaded prop replaces the client's value. Merge props tell the client to combine them. This is how pagination, chat messages and incremental lists work. C\ Metadata Client behavior --- --- --- Merge(v) mergeProps: ["key"] Append to the existing array Prop(...).Prepend() prependProps: ["key"] Prepend Merge(v).Append("path") mergeProps: ["key.path"] Append at a nested path Prop(...).Prepend("path") prependProps: ["key.path"] Prepend at a nested path DeepMerge(v) deepMergeProps: ["key"] Deep merge objects and arrays .MatchOn("id") matchPropsOn: ["key.id"] Replace items with the same id instead of duplicating them .Append("path", matchOn: "id") matchPropsOn: ["key.path.id"] The match key is relative to the nested path Nested paths The path before the wrapper stays on the client; only the value below the path is merged. Resetting a merge The client can ask for a fresh value instead of a merge by listing the path in X-Inertia-Reset : Metadata is skipped for paths in the reset list, and on partial reloads for paths the reload did not ask for. Match on a stable key .MatchOn("id") replaces an item with the same key instead of appending a duplicate. Use a stable, unique key from your data. Without it, incremental updates append every item again. Deep merge DeepMerge recursively combines objects. Arrays are merged by index; use MatchOn when you need item identity. On a partial reload, merge metadata is only emitted for paths the reload asked for. Always still applies independently.

title: Redirects and history
description: Redirects, Back, Location, history encryption, clearing and URL fragments.
body: Inertia requests follow redirects with XHR, which is not always what the browser would do. Inertia.Net adjusts redirect responses so the client behaves correctly. Redirect helpers Back() follows a Referer only when it is an http(s) URL with the request's own host and port. When it is unavailable, the opt-in previous URL is tried before the fallback. This prevents an open redirect. The scheme is not compared, so it works behind a TLS-terminating proxy; on HTTPS an http Referer is upgraded to https . Previous URL If a form returns Back() but the browser does not send its previous address ( Referer ), enable this option. For example, it helps when your site uses Referrer-Policy: no-referrer : After a successful page visit, a later Back() can use that saved address. Back() and the middleware's empty-response redirect consult the same-host Referer first, then the remembered URL, then the fallback. context.Inertia().PreviousUrl reads the remembered URL, or returns null when disabled, absent or invalid; it is user-controlled input validated as a relative path. Only successful status-200 page GET renders are remembered, including initial HTML visits. Partial reloads, prefetches, Precognition, non-GET requests and error pages are excluded. The value is the relative PathBase + Path + QueryString , without scheme or host, in the plain .Inertia.Previous session cookie ( HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , Path=/ , essential, with Secure following o.State.CookieSecurePolicy ). The cookie is written only when the URL changes. Set o.State.PreviousUrlCookieName to change its name; it must differ from o.State.CookieName . This cookie is used with both cookie and session state stores. It is per browser, not per tab : the most recent page render wins across tabs. The Referer still takes precedence when available. What the middleware changes Situation Result --- --- 302 for PUT, PATCH or DELETE Changed to 303 See Other , so the browser follows with a GET Redirect to another origin, non-prefetch 409 with X-Inertia-Location : the client makes a full visit instead of an XHR the browser would block Redirect whose Location contains , non-prefetch 409 with X-Inertia-Redirect : the client performs a full visit that keeps the fragment Location(url) 409 + X-Inertia-Location for Inertia requests, a plain 302 otherwise Empty 200 response Redirect back (302, or 303 for PUT/PATCH/DELETE), using the same previous-URL and app-root fallback as Back() Vary Vary: X-Inertia is added to every response through the middleware Turn off external redirect conversion with o.ConvertExternalRedirects = false if the app intentionally redirects to another origin. Pages without a handler Maps GET and HEAD to Render("About", props) , like Laravel's Route::inertia . In MVC, return this.InertiaView(props); renders the action's own component, {Controller}/{Action} by default. AddInertiaMvc(o = o.ComponentResolver = ctx = ...) changes the rule. History encryption encryptHistory is written as true only when set and is not carried across redirects. The Inertia client encrypts its history state with the page's key. Clearing history clearHistory goes through the state store, applies to the next page rendered after the redirect(s), then is consumed. It is typically used before a redirect after logout. Preserving a fragment By default a redirect loses the URL fragment. PreserveFragment() keeps it across the next redirect. The client receives preserveFragment: true on the next page. Page URL The page object's url is PathBase, Path and QueryString. Behind a proxy that rewrites paths, set o.UrlResolver to return the URL the browser sees: Flash data, errors, clearHistory and preserveFragment share the state store. By default that is an encrypted cookie; see Flash data.

title: Deferred props
description: Load slow page sections after the first render, in groups.
body: Defer leaves a prop out of the first response and lists it under deferredProps . The client requests each group with a partial reload as soon as the page is mounted. The page becomes interactive without waiting for the slow data. A deferred prop can also be live: it is fetched again whenever its event is broadcast. Props in the same group load in one request. Different groups load in parallel requests. deferredProps is only produced on non-partial renders. The client The fallback is a prop in React, a fallback slot in Vue and a fallback snippet in Svelte. Combining with other props A deferred prop can also be merged, once or rescued: The metadata combines: deferredProps lists the group, mergeProps lists the path, and onceProps records the key. Deferred scroll props A deferred Scroll(...) prop reports "posts.data" just like a resolved one. This is a deliberate fix of an inertia-laravel quirk: Testing See Testing for the full assertion API. Deferred props are for data the page can render without. If the page cannot be meaningful until the data arrives, a normal prop is simpler.

title: Typed routes
description: Generate a typed routes.ts for named endpoints, with typed parameters and request bodies, and write it at build time.
body: This builds on TypeScript types: the same o.TypeScript options write both files. Routes come from endpoint names, so they work the same whether an endpoint renders with Render("Component", props) or a page record. Generate routes.ts Set RoutesOutputPath and every named endpoint ( WithName , a controller route name, or a FastEndpoints Description(x = x.WithName(...)) ) gets a typed function in routes.ts : - Route parameters are typed from their constraints; optional and catch-all parameters are optional. - Every HTTP method of an endpoint has a variant ( routes.users.update.put(1) ). - routeConfig.base prefixes every URL (an app under a path base). - RouteBodies holds the [FromBody] (or FastEndpoints request) type of each route that has one. - Unnamed endpoints are skipped. o.TypeScript.LiveEvents(...) also exports live event names and channels as liveEvents . See Live props. To assert a route sent as a prop in tests, use WhereRoute(key, url, method) . See Testing. Generating at build time Set true in the project file, and every build (including the one inside dotnet publish ) runs the app once with --inertia-types to write both files. The app starts without listening on any port and exits; a failure to write fails the build. In CI, compare the result with the committed files: Component names are checked at compile time too. See Page records.

title: Configuration
description: InertiaOptions, Vite, SSR, props, state and the middleware and result API.
body: Core configuration is passed to AddInertia ; error page options use AddInertiaErrorPages . Options marked “Development only” do nothing in other environments. AddInertia(o = ...) : InertiaOptions Option Default Description --- --- --- RootView "app.html" Root template relative to the content root (a Razor view name with UseRazorRootView ). Paths outside the content root are refused. RootElementId "app" Id of the root element and the data-page script. Version null Asset version. null means the Vite manifest hash, or "" without one. VersionResolver null Func per-request version; wins over Version when non-null. EncryptHistory false Encrypt browser history state of every page. WithAllErrors false Send every validation message per field instead of the first. PreserveBigIntegers false Emit integers beyond ±(2^53−1) as {"$bigint":"..."} . ExposeSharedPropKeys true List top-level shared keys in sharedProps . CspNonce null Func : the request's CSP nonce. ConvertExternalRedirects true Turn an Inertia redirect to another origin into 409 + X-Inertia-Location . UrlResolver null Func : the page url . Pages.Directory / Pages.Extensions null / .tsx .jsx .ts .js .vue .svelte Development check that a rendered component has a page file. TypeScript.OutputPath , .Page (component) , .SharedProps () , .FlashData () null TypeScript declarations, written in Development. Share(key, value) / Share(key, Func ) none Shared props. o.Pagination : PaginationOptions Option Default Description --- --- --- DefaultPerPage 20 Default page size. MaxPerPage 100 Maximum page size (below int.MaxValue to allow over-fetching); the default must be between 1 and this value. PageName "page" Numbered-page query parameter. PerPageName "perPage" Page-size query parameter. CursorName "cursor" Cursor query parameter. o.Vite : ViteOptions Option Default Description --- --- --- PublicDirectory "wwwroot" Web root containing the build directory and hot file. BuildDirectory "build" Vite output directory under PublicDirectory ; also the URL prefix. ManifestPath null Manifest path relative to the content root. null = {PublicDirectory}/{BuildDirectory}/.vite/manifest.json , then manifest.json . HotFilePath null Hot file relative to the content root. null = {PublicDirectory}/hot . Read in Development only. DevServerUrl null Dev server origin, e.g. http://localhost:5173 . When set, dev tags always render. AssetBaseUrl null Replaces {PathBase}/{BuildDirectory} as the URL prefix of built assets. Prefetch None Waterfall or Aggressive : prefetch code-split chunks after load. PrefetchConcurrency 3 Chunks Waterfall downloads at a time. o.Ssr : SsrOptions Ssr.ConnectTimeout bounds connection establishment separately from the rendering deadline and defaults to five seconds; use a positive supported duration or Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan . Option Default Description --- --- --- Mode Disabled Disabled , Preferred or Required . Disabled cannot be overridden per response. Urls empty ( http://127.0.0.1:13714 ) SSR server base URLs. Not used with UseNodeProcess() . Timeout 5 s Total deadline per render. Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan disables it. MaxResponseBytes 16 MiB Limit on actual response bytes, including errors and chunked responses. MaxPageBytes 2 MiB Pages whose JSON is larger render on the client without a call. BundlePath null Skip SSR while this file is missing, unless the Vite dev server runs. ExcludePaths empty Request paths never rendered on the server (exact, or a trailing for a prefix). Concurrency.MaxActive 8 Renders in flight per server from this app instance; 0 for no limit. Concurrency.MaxQueued 32 Renders waiting for a slot per server. Concurrency.QueueTimeout 250 ms How long a render waits for a slot. CircuitBreaker.Enabled true Pause servers that keep failing. CircuitBreaker.FailureThreshold 5 Consecutive failures that open a server's circuit. CircuitBreaker.BreakDuration 10 s How long an open circuit skips the server before one probe. Cache.Duration Zero (off) Reuse a render for this long when the page JSON is the same. Cache.StaleFor Zero Serve stale while re-rendering. Cache.MaxBytes 64 MiB Size of the default store's render cache. UseNodeProcess(configure?) off Start and supervise Node SSR processes (sets Mode = Preferred when Disabled ). Per response: Render(...).WithSsr(SsrMode) and .WithoutSsr() . The full SSR options are in Server-side rendering. o.Props : InertiaPropsOptions Option Default Description --- --- --- MaxConcurrency 4 Loaders marked .Parallel() that run at once per render. Must be positive. o.State : InertiaStateOptions Option Default Description --- --- --- CookieName ".Inertia.State" Cookie name (cookie store) or session key (session store). RememberPreviousUrl false Remember successful page GET URLs for Back() when Referer is unavailable. PreviousUrlCookieName ".Inertia.Previous" Plain previous-URL cookie, with either state store; non-empty and different from CookieName . CookieSecurePolicy SameAsRequest When state and previous-URL cookies are Secure . UseSession() off Use ISession instead of the encrypted cookie. AddInertiaMvc(o = o.UseTempDataStateStore()) off Use MVC TempData. Inertia.Net.Mvc package. AddInertiaErrorPages(o = ...) : InertiaErrorPagesOptions Option Default Description --- --- --- Component "Error" Default error component. Components empty Per-status overrides, with keys in StatusCodes . StatusCodes [403, 404, 500, 503] Non-empty set of statuses from 400–599. Protocol 409 and antiforgery 419 responses are preserved. EnabledInDevelopment false Preview error components in Development. Props null Func for additional props. See Error pages for setup, shared props and existing exception middleware. Middleware and endpoint API API Description --- --- services.AddInertia(configure?) Registers services and options. services.AddInertiaErrorPages(configure?) / app.UseInertiaErrorPages(useExceptionHandler: true) Error page services and middleware, before UseInertia() . Use false with your own UseExceptionHandler() . app.UseInertia() The protocol middleware. Before the endpoints; after UseSession() when used. app.UseInertiaAntiforgery(configure?) Issues the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and validates unsafe requests ( 419 on failure). app.MapInertia(pattern, component, props?) GET and HEAD endpoint that renders the component. services.AddInertiaDevTools(configure?) / app.MapInertiaDevTools() DevTools recorder and read API. A warning is logged when recording is enabled outside Development without an Authorize callback; the read API then returns 404. app.UseInertiaAntiforgeryCookie(cookieName = "XSRF-TOKEN") Only writes the token cookie; validation is up to you. endpoint.WithInertiaValidation() Minimal API: validation failures redirect back with errors. endpoint.WithInertiaPrecognition() Minimal API: WithInertiaValidation() plus Precognition. healthChecks.AddInertiaSsr(...) SSR health check from the gateway's state. mvc.AddInertiaMvc(o = o.UseRazorRootView("App")) MVC filter, optional Razor root view and component resolver. config.ConfigureInertia(configure?) FastEndpoints: validation redirect and Precognition. Render(component, props?) InertiaResult : .WithStatusCode , .WithRootView , .WithViewData , .WithSsr , .WithoutSsr , .WithSsrCache .
