Location(url) InertiaLocationResult . Back(fallback = "~/") InertiaBackResult : .WithErrors , .WithFlash . httpContext.Inertia() InertiaFeature : Share , Flash , WithErrors , ClearHistory , EncryptHistory , PreserveFragment . Send.InertiaAsync(...) , Send.InertiaLocationAsync(...) , Send.InertiaBackAsync(...) FastEndpoints Send extensions. Extension points IInertiaRootView , IInertiaStateStore , ViteAssets , InertiaRequest (parsed headers), InertiaHeaders (header name constants), InertiaSsrException , InertiaSsr.HttpClientName (the SSR HTTP client) and InertiaDiagnostics (meter and activity source names). Name collisions The package imports Inertia.Net and static members of Inertia.Net.Inertia when implicit usings are enabled. If a name such as Location collides with a type, use Inertia.Net.Inertia.Location(url) . To manage imports yourself, set false in the project and add using Inertia.Net; and using static Inertia.Net.Inertia; where needed. InertiaPropJsonConverter , InertiaSsrHealthCheck , InertiaCacheEntryKind , InertiaCacheEntryOptions , InertiaPagesOptions , InertiaPrecognition.IsPrecognitive(...) and InertiaPrecognitionMetadata are public APIs for serialization, health checks, cache stores, page checks and precognitive request handling.

title: Redis cache
description: Share cached props and SSR renders between app instances with the Inertia.Net.Redis cache store.
body: Inertia.Net.Redis keeps cached props ( .Cache(...) ) and SSR renders in Redis, so every app instance shares them and one instance's IInertiaCache.RemoveByTagAsync clears them for all. The default prefix is inertia.net: . How entries are stored - Each entry is a Redis string with the entry's expiration. Each tag is a set of entry keys that lives as long as its longest entry, and each entry keeps an index of its tags. - Storing or removing an entry is one script, so a removal racing a store leaves the entry either removed or whole and still tagged. - Removing a tag works in batches, so a tag on every entry does not block the server. Put a hash tag in the prefix ( {myapp}: ): an entry, its index and its tag sets change together in one script. Failures Failures are not swallowed. While a page renders, Inertia.Net logs a failing store (rate-limited) and renders without the cache: the loaders run, as on a miss. IInertiaCache calls throw, so a failed invalidation is not silent. Native AOT The Redis store is not verified under Native AOT. See the package README and Deploying behind a proxy for the rest of the multi-instance setup.

title: Head tags
description: Set the page title, meta and link tags on the server, in the first HTML response and on every visit.
headings: A title template and per-request tags
body: Set the page's , meta and link tags on the server. They are in the first HTML response (no JavaScript needed, so crawlers and link previews see them) and travel with every visit as the head prop. A title template and per-request tags On the client Put @inertiaHead (or in Razor) before the template's own . See the root template. How tags are keyed - Values are HTML-encoded. - Each tag is keyed ( data-inertia ) by title , the meta name or property, or the link rel. A later call with the same key replaces the tag, and Remove(key) drops one set earlier (for example by middleware). - With SSR the server-rendered head is used, which the client builds from the same prop. - o.Head.PropName renames the prop. In tests, HasHead("title", "Users - App") asserts a tag. See Testing.

title: Pages and responses
description: Render components, use MapInertia, and understand the root template and response status codes.
body: An Inertia page is a component name plus a set of props. The server writes the page object into the response; the client resolves the component and renders it. Rendering a page Render(component, props) returns an InertiaResult . The component name must match your client-side page resolver exactly, including case. Render accepts an InertiaProps (an ordered string-keyed dictionary), any IDictionary , or a typed object whose properties are the props. Nested InertiaProps and dictionaries are walked at any depth. This is the default style, and the rest of these docs use it. If you want typed props, a record that implements IInertiaPage names its component, so Render(new UsersPage(...)) needs no component string, and the record can hold its own GET handler. See Page records. Every page has an errors prop (an empty object when there are no errors). Key order is errors , shared props, then page props. Every response is one of three things, depending on how the request arrived: Per-response options InertiaResult builds on the response without changing the component: Method Effect --- --- .WithStatusCode(int) Sets the HTTP status of the page response .WithRootView(string) Uses another root template for this response .WithViewData(key, value) Makes a value available to @viewData("key") .WithSsr(SsrMode) / .WithoutSsr() Overrides the SSR mode for this response .WithSsrCache(duration, staleFor?) Reuses a server-rendered response for the same page JSON Pages without a handler MapInertia maps GET and HEAD to a rendered page, like Laravel's Route::inertia : The root template On the first visit the response is an HTML document. Inertia.Net reads app.html from the content root (configurable with RootView ), parses it once, and replaces these tokens: Token Output --- --- @inertia Without SSR: the page JSON script and the root element. With SSR: the server-rendered body. Required. @inertiaHead The SSR head tags joined with newlines. Empty without SSR. @vite("resources/js/app.tsx") Vite tags for one or more comma-separated entries. @viteReactRefresh The React Fast Refresh preamble while the dev server runs. Put it before @vite . @viewData("title") An HTML-encoded value passed with WithViewData . @@ A literal @ . Other @ characters, such as CSS at-rules and e-mail addresses, are left alone. Arguments accept single or double quotes. The page JSON is escaped with \uXXXX sequences, so a prop containing cannot break out of the script element. RootElementId (default app ) changes both the root element id and the data-page value. The client finds the page script by that id. app.html is read from disk at runtime. Add CopyToOutputDirectory and CopyToPublishDirectory so it is present after dotnet publish . Razor root view (MVC) With Inertia.Net.Mvc , the first-visit HTML can be a Razor view: "App" finds Views/Shared/App.cshtml . The view receives an InertiaRootViewContext model and uses tag helpers: takes comma-separated entries. SSR runs at most once per request and is shared by and . WithRootView("Other") takes Razor view names when the Razor root view is enabled. A custom root view Implement IInertiaRootView and register it before AddInertia : Page URL and path base The page object's url is the request PathBase, Path and QueryString. Behind a proxy that rewrites paths, set o.UrlResolver to return the URL the browser sees: Back() and the Vite asset URLs also respect the path base.

title: Installation
description: Install Inertia.Net, the optional MVC, FastEndpoints, SignalR, Redis or MongoDB package, and the testing helpers.
body: Inertia.Net is split into small packages. Install the core package and one optional backend integration. Package Install when --- --- Inertia.Net always. The core adapter, Minimal API support, Vite, SSR, state store and antiforgery Inertia.Net.Mvc you use MVC controllers: ModelState filter, Razor root view and tag helpers Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints you use FastEndpoints: Send extensions, validation pre-processor and Precognition Inertia.Net.Live.SignalR you deliver live props over SignalR: hub, channel authorization and broadcaster Inertia.Net.EntityFrameworkCore you page EF Core queries with numbered or cursor pagination Inertia.Net.Redis you share cached props and SSR renders between app instances through Redis Inertia.Net.MongoDB you page MongoDB finds with numbered or cursor pagination Inertia.Net.Testing in your test project: fluent assertions over Inertia responses Inertia.Net.Templates dotnet new install Inertia.Net.Templates : start a complete app Use the same version for every Inertia.Net package. The package version and the Inertia.js protocol version are separate numbers: Inertia.Net 1.9.4 implements Inertia.js v3. Requirements - .NET 10 or .NET 11 SDK and an Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web project. - JavaScript frontend build tools with npm, Bun, pnpm or Yarn. Managed SSR requires Node.js or Bun at runtime. - An Inertia.js v3 client: @inertiajs/react , @inertiajs/vue3 or @inertiajs/svelte . .NET 10 and .NET 11 Every package ships net10.0 and net11.0 assemblies, and NuGet picks the one that matches your app. Things to know on .NET 11: - Use 1.8.0 or later on .NET 11. Inertia.Net 1.7.1 and earlier were built against .NET 10 only. .NET 11 reshaped the experimental resolver API of Microsoft.Extensions.Validation , so WithInertiaValidation() and WithInertiaPrecognition() from 1.7.1 fail on .NET 11 with TypeLoadException: Could not load type 'Microsoft.Extensions.Validation.IValidatableInfo' . - Retarget, don't roll forward. A net10.0 app that calls AddValidation() and runs on the .NET 11 runtime ( DOTNET ROLL FORWARD=LatestMajor ) fails whatever adapter it uses: the validation source generator wrote .NET 10 types that .NET 11 removed. Set net11.0 and rebuild. - Dependencies follow the target framework. On net11.0 , Inertia.Net.EntityFrameworkCore depends on EF Core 11 and Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints on FastEndpoints 9; on net10.0 they use EF Core 10.0.15 and FastEndpoints 8.3.0. Reference the FastEndpoints.Generator version that matches your FastEndpoints version. - Async validators. AsyncValidationAttribute and IAsyncValidatableObject errors go through WithInertiaValidation() and WithInertiaPrecognition() like synchronous ones. See Validation and errors. - Automatic CSRF check. Apps built with WebApplication.CreateBuilder also get the framework's Sec-Fetch-Site / Origin check. UseInertiaAntiforgery() is still the token check Inertia needs. See CSRF and antiforgery. - C 15 unions work as props and in the generated TypeScript. See Props and TypeScript. - Compression. AddResponseCompression() also offers Zstandard and always adds Vary: Accept-Encoding ; Inertia's Vary: X-Inertia stays next to it. Start from the template Choose --framework vue or --framework svelte for another client, and add --auth for cookie sign-in (see Authentication). The template includes working pages, a Todos form, validation, flash messages, CSRF protection and Vite configuration. The app targets .NET 10 (LTS) by default; add --tfm net11.0 to target .NET 11. Install dependencies, then start Vite using the package manager chosen for your app. All four are supported: Package manager Install dependencies Start Vite Build assets --- --- --- --- npm npm install npm run dev npm run build Bun bun install bun run dev bun run build pnpm pnpm install pnpm run dev pnpm run build Yarn yarn install yarn run dev yarn run build Keep Vite running and start ASP.NET Core in another terminal with dotnet watch . For production, run your row's build command, then dotnet publish -c Release . Keep the lockfile for the package manager you choose. Namespace and global usings The namespace is Inertia.Net and the static factory class is Inertia.Net.Inertia . C resolves a leading Inertia to the namespace, so Inertia.Render(...) does not compile outside the Inertia.Net namespace. The package's buildTransitive props file adds both global usings when enable is set, which is the default in new projects: Write Render(...) , Defer(...) , Once(...) , Back() and Location(...) unqualified. Set false and add using static Inertia.Net.Inertia; yourself, or call Inertia.Net.Inertia.Render(...) . HttpContext.Inertia() is an extension method and works as written. Next steps Add the four pieces every Inertia app needs: services, middleware, a root template and a client. Install React, Vue or Svelte and configure Vite for development and production.

title: TypeScript types
description: Generate declarations for page props, shared props and flash data from your .NET contracts.
body: Inertia.Net can write TypeScript declarations for typed page props, shared props and flash data. They follow the app's JSON contracts (the HTTP JSON options and their source-generated contexts), so names, nullability and enum values match the page JSON. To name a page's component once, see Page records. To generate a typed routes.ts for your named endpoints, see Typed routes. Configure generation The file is written when the app starts in Development, and only when its content changed. Commit it so tsc passes in CI without running the app. Generate in CI To write the file without starting the app for real (in CI, or outside Development), run it with --inertia-types : it writes the declarations in any environment, then stops, and exits with code 1 if they could not be written. The templates add it as a script: Program.cs still runs up to app.Run() , so startup code such as migrations runs too; the server stops as soon as it has started. Shared props Shared props are inferred from the values passed to o.Share(...) ; dot keys nest. A factory is typed by what it returns: o.Share("user", ctx = new UserDto(...)) gives user: UserDto , while a factory cast to Func is unknown . Shares added per request (middleware, HttpContext.Inertia().Share(...) ) are not known at startup; type them with o.TypeScript.SharedProps () , which replaces the inference with an explicit type. The InertiaConfig augmentation types usePage().props and flash . Flash data FlashData () types the whole flash object, not one entry: each property of T is a flash key. To type Flash("toast", new Toast("success", "Saved")) , wrap the entry: Prop members An InertiaProp member is optional (it can be deferred, optional or rescued) and unknown , unless [InertiaPropType(typeof(T))] names its value type. Mapping .NET TypeScript --- --- int , long , double , decimal , float number ( number \ bigint for 64-bit and larger with PreserveBigIntegers ) DateTime , DateTimeOffset , DateOnly , TimeOnly , Guid , byte[] string enum union of JSON values: numbers by default, with the member names in a doc comment; string names with JsonStringEnumConverter dictionary Record polymorphic type union tagged with its discriminator C 15 union (.NET 11) union of its case types, User \ Team (plus \ null when a case is nullable) nullable member T \ null Types missing from the JSON metadata (under Native AOT, register them in your context) are unknown , with a warning in the log. Number handling follows member settings, then type settings, then the global JSON options. Custom converter output is typed as unknown with a warning when its shape cannot be inferred. Props and MVC validation error keys use the HTTP JsonOptions . FastEndpoints error keys use its binding serializer policy. Keep client field names aligned with the applicable policy; custom resolvers without member metadata may require client JSON names for aliases.

title: Testing
description: Fluent assertions over Inertia responses and helpers for partial reloads and deferred props.
body: Inertia.Net.Testing has Laravel-style fluent assertions over Inertia responses and HttpClient helpers. It parses both JSON responses ( X-Inertia: true ) and the first-visit HTML , and decodes $bigint values. Failures throw InertiaAssertionException with a readable message, so it works with any test framework. Add public partial class Program; to your app when it uses top-level statements. To check that an error page keeps its HTTP status, use Status with the response's page assertion: Test host recipe With WebApplicationFactory , pin the asset version so requests need no first visit to learn it, and turn SSR off so tests need no Node server: For form posts, read the XSRF token from a page response with GetXsrfToken() and send it with WithXsrfToken() (see Testing a form with antiforgery). A cookie-keeping client ( factory.CreateClient(new() { AllowAutoRedirect = false, HandleCookies = true }) ) holds the antiforgery cookie and the sign-in cookie between requests. Request helpers Helper Purpose --- --- InertiaGetAsync(url, version?, configure?) Sends an Inertia GET InertiaRequestAsync(method, url, content?, version?, configure?) Sends an Inertia request with any method GetInertiaPageAsync() Parses the response into an InertiaPage AssertInertiaAsync(assert) Parses, runs the assertions and returns the page Page assertions Component , Url , Version , HasFlash(key) , HasFlash(key, value) , MissingFlash(key) , HasDeferred(path) , HasDeferred(group, path) , HasLive(path) and HasLive(path, channel, event) for live props (the channel as "{type}:{name}" , e.g. private:orders.1 ), and HasHead(key) or HasHead(key, contains) for head tags, keyed like the tags' data-inertia attribute ( title , a meta name or property, a link rel): Prop assertions On props and nested scopes (dot paths and array indexes allowed): Has(key) , Has(key, count) , Has(key, scope) , Has(key, count, firstItemScope) , HasAll , HasAny , Missing , MissingAll , Where(key, value) , Where(key, predicate) , WhereNot , WhereNull , WhereNotNull , WhereType(key, "string null") , WhereAllType , WhereContains(key, ...) , Count , CountBetween , Each(scope) , First(scope) and Dump() . WhereRoute(key, url, method) asserts a route sent as a prop in the client's { url, method } shape, which is what the generated routes.ts functions return. The method defaults to get and is compared ignoring case: Strict interaction tracking. Like Laravel, a nested scope fails when it contains properties you did not assert, unless you end it with Etc() . The root scope is not checked automatically: call .Interacted() at the end to enforce that every top-level prop was asserted. Partial reloads and deferred props InertiaPage replays the request with the right headers: HasScroll(path) asserts scroll metadata; HasScroll(path, currentPage, nextPage) also checks the page values. The page helpers use the metadata and send the appropriate append or prepend intent. ReloadOnlyAsync asserts that "users" is in the result; ReloadExceptAsync asserts that it is missing. InertiaPage members Props , Raw , Prop(path) , HasProp(path) , PropBigInteger(path) , DeferredProps , MergeProps , PrependProps , DeepMergeProps , MatchPropsOn , RescuedProps , SharedProps , ScrollProps , OnceProps , LiveProps , Flash , EncryptHistory , ClearHistory , PreserveFragment , PreserveBigIntegers . Flash and errors travel in a cookie across the redirect, so use a client that keeps cookies. Disable AllowAutoRedirect to assert the redirect itself, then follow it with a second InertiaGetAsync to read the flash or errors. Testing a form with antiforgery Keep cookies and disable redirects on the test client. Load the form first, then send its XSRF token on the Inertia POST and follow the redirect: Import System.Net and System.Net.Http.Json . For a named bag use HasErrorBag("createUser") and HasError("email", bag: "createUser") . Dotted keys such as items.0.email are matched as flat error keys; with all errors enabled a message assertion matches any message. GetXsrfToken() and WithXsrfToken() accept custom cookie and header names. The cookie container must retain the antiforgery cookie as well as the Inertia state cookie.

title: Pagination
description: Create numbered and cursor pages for pagers and infinite scroll.
body: A long list is easier to browse when the server sends a small group of items at a time. A numbered page lets readers choose a page; a cursor page uses a marker to fetch the next or previous group. Start with a list already in memory: Visiting /posts?page=2&perPage=5 returns the second group in posts.data . The default page size is 20 and the maximum is 100; configure both in Pagination options. For infinite scroll, wrap that value in Scroll(...) and render it with InfiniteScroll as shown in Infinite scroll. Pagination creates page values; Scroll adds infinite-scroll metadata and merging. Use a page directly for a classic pager. You write You get --- --- Pagination.Paginate(posts, request) A numbered Page for a pager Scroll(Pagination.Paginate(posts, request)) Numbered infinite scroll Scroll(await Pagination.PaginateAsync(request, key, fetch, ct: ct)) Cursor-based infinite scroll using your data source Scroll(ct = Pagination.PaginateAsync(request, fetch, ct: ct)).Defer() A deferred page; other prop modifiers also work Minimal API handlers can take PageRequest or CursorRequest directly, as in Infinite scroll. MVC and FastEndpoints can call PageRequest.From(Request.Query) and CursorRequest.From(HttpContext) . Page numbers below 1 become 1; invalid page sizes use the default and sizes above the maximum are clamped. Set defaults and parameter names with o.Pagination in AddInertia . From and BindAsync retain the query parameter name for the returned page. An explicit paginator name overrides it. Pagination.Paginate slices an already materialized IReadOnlyList . For a database, search SDK or HTTP API, Pagination.PaginateAsync accepts a fetch(skip, take, ct) delegate and an optional count delegate. It requests one extra item to determine hasMore ; without a count, total and lastPage are null. Delegate offsets above int.MaxValue return an empty page without calling fetch ; the optional count still runs. Supply a stable, fully unique ordering to your data source. For a classic pager, use currentPage , lastPage , and pageName to build links; pages do not contain URL links. from and to are one-based and null on an empty page. The examples abbreviate the data array. For example, a data source can implement numbered pages without exposing IQueryable : For a pager, use Inertia links and preserve any other filters your app needs: Cursors A cursor is a marker for the position of an item, useful when readers move forward and backward rather than jump to page numbers. The cursor overload of PaginateAsync takes a key selector and a fetch delegate. The delegate receives a decoded cursor with Direction ( After or Before ) and Value , a take count, and a cancellation token. Return rows in the requested direction, including up to one extra; the helper trims and reverses Before results to display order. Choose a stable unique non-null key. hasMore indicates more rows in the requested direction. Cursors are URL-safe base64 of a compact JSON array: direction ( "a" or "b" ) followed by the key values. Supported keys are int , long , Guid , string , DateTime , DateTimeOffset , decimal , double , and bool . Cursors are not tamper-proof ; apps that need tamper protection should wrap them with IDataProtector . A malformed or foreign nonempty cursor falls back to the first page. When CursorRequest.Logger is set, the paginator logs this at Debug without cursor values or exception details. Minimal API binding uses configured pagination options and supplies a logger in the Inertia.Net.Pagination category when a logger factory is available. In MVC or FastEndpoints, CursorRequest.From(HttpContext) does the same; optional arguments override the configured defaults and parameter names. For a query-only request or a request created outside HTTP, supply an app logger explicitly: Logger is ignored by JSON serialization and does not affect request equality. Defer or cache a page A page can use the same prop modifiers as other values. For example, Scroll(ct = Pagination.PaginateAsync(request, fetch, ct: ct)).Defer() loads it after the first response; a lazy prop can also use .Cache(...) . See Deferred props and Props for loader and cache options. With EF Core If your app uses EF Core, install the optional package alongside your database provider: The following uses an existing AppDb as db , with a Posts set. request is a PageRequest , cursorRequest is a CursorRequest , and ct is the request cancellation token: Both results contain the selected group in data . A cursor is a marker: send it back unchanged to request the next or previous group. ToPageAsync requires an ordered query and counts rows by default; pass countTotal: false to skip the count and return null total and lastPage . ToCursorPageAsync rejects an already ordered query and orders by the supplied key and optional tie-breaker itself. Both guards throw InvalidOperationException . The cursor helper fetches in both directions without counting. Choose a stable, fully unique ordering: use a unique key, or add a unique tie-breaker when the first key can repeat. Nullable keys are unsupported. The cursor codec supports the types listed above, but EF translation and ordering for each type depend on the database provider; for example, SQLite needs a suitable value conversion to order DateTimeOffset . The name from a bound request or From(...) is used for the corresponding page parameter; an explicit pageName or cursorName argument takes precedence. The EF Core package is not marked Native AOT compatible. EF Core has its own compiled-model requirements; for Native AOT applications, use the core delegate paginators with an AOT-compatible data source instead. With MongoDB Inertia.Net.MongoDB builds the same Page and CursorPage values from a collection.Find(filter) : The rules are those of the EF Core helpers: - ToPageAsync needs a sorted find (skip and limit are replaced) and counts the filter with CountDocuments unless countTotal: false . - ToCursorPageAsync needs an unsorted find: it adds the keyset condition to the find's filter and sorts by the key (and tie-breaker). Keys may be ObjectId (held in the cursor as its 24-character string), int , long , string , Guid , DateTime , DateTimeOffset , decimal , double or bool . A tampered or unparseable cursor starts at the first page. - MongoDB orders strings by their UTF-8 bytes. The MongoDB driver does not support trimming or Native AOT, so neither does this package. See the package README. Native AOT Register each closed page type in your app's JsonSerializerContext along with the item types: See Native AOT. Caching and scroll props A cached page still writes its scroll metadata. Use cache keys that include the page or cursor and all user or tenant dependencies. Scroll(...) can be deferred or cached; do not reuse its mutable prop instance across requests. Root Append() and Prepend() cannot be combined on the same prop. See Props and Infinite scroll.

title: Why Inertia?
description: What Inertia is, how it compares to React, Vue or Svelte with a Web API, and the features and prop types Inertia.Net adds.
headings: Inertia vs a SPA plus a Web API
Why a .NET developer might like it
When it is not a good fit
body: The short version If you build a React, Vue or Svelte frontend on ASP.NET Core today, you probably have two projects: a Web API that returns JSON, and a single-page app (SPA) that calls it. Inertia lets you keep the modern frontend and drop the second half of that setup. Your endpoint does not return JSON. It returns the name of a frontend page and the data that page needs : The matching component receives that data as ordinary props: The first visit is a normal HTML response. After that, links and form submissions fetch the next page's props in the background and swap the component without a full reload. It feels like a SPA, but ASP.NET Core still owns routing, authentication and validation. Choose it when one team ships the frontend and backend together: dashboards, admin tools, SaaS products, internal apps. Skip it when you need a public JSON API for mobile apps or third parties, or the frontend is a separate product with its own release cycle. Want to see it run? Try First 10 minutes. Want the details? Keep reading. How a request works The first visit returns HTML. Every later click is an X-Inertia request that returns only JSON, so the page never reloads. ' }, { from: 0, to: 0, text: 'Client app boots and renders the page' }, { from: 0, to: 1, text: 'Click a link: GET /users/1', code: 'X-Inertia: true', phase: 'Every click after' }, { from: 1, to: 2, text: 'Run the route' }, { from: 2, to: 1, text: 'Same Render call', reply: true }, { from: 1, to: 0, text: 'Only the page object, as JSON', reply: true, code: '{ "component": "Users/Show", "props": {...} }' }, { from: 0, to: 0, text: 'Swap the page component, no reload' }, ]} / In more detail Inertia vs a SPA plus a Web API SPA + Web API Inertia.Net --- --- --- Projects to build and deploy A JSON API and a separate client app, often with different hosts and CORS rules One ASP.NET Core app that also builds your frontend Routing A server router for the API and a client router for pages, kept in sync by hand ASP.NET Core routes only. Each route renders a page Data loading Fetch calls, loading states and caching in each component Props arrive with the page. Slow data can be deferred Authentication Tokens or cookies shared across two apps, plus client-side route guards Your normal ASP.NET Core cookie auth and [Authorize] Validation Return an error shape from the API and map it to forms in the client Redirect back with errors, available as form.errors (validation) API contract You design, version and document JSON endpoints The props you pass are the contract. TypeScript types can be generated Frontend React, Vue or Svelte React, Vue or Svelte You still write components, hooks and styles. What goes away is the glue: the API layer, the client router, and the code that keeps state in sync with the server. Why a .NET developer might like it - Minimal APIs, MVC controllers and FastEndpoints stay in charge. Model binding, authorization, validation attributes and dependency injection work as they always have. - One deployment. dotnet publish produces the server and the built frontend assets together. - Security defaults you already know. CSRF protection, cookies and policies are ASP.NET Core's, with antiforgery wired up for you. - Pages are real URLs. Links, refresh, back and bookmarks behave, and optional server-side rendering renders the first visit's HTML on the server. Features Area What you get Learn more --- --- --- Backends Minimal APIs, MVC controllers and FastEndpoints on one core package Quick start Clients React, Vue and Svelte with the Inertia.js v3 client Client setup Shared data Props sent with every page, such as the signed-in user, set statically or per request Shared data Validation Redirect back with errors before your handler runs, with named error bags Validation Precognition Validate a form before it is submitted, without running the handler Precognition Flash data One-time messages or typed values that survive a redirect Flash data Redirects and history Back() , Location() , external redirects, history encryption and clearing Redirects and history Error pages Routing failures and unhandled exceptions rendered as Inertia pages Error pages Asset versioning The client reloads once when your JavaScript or CSS changes Asset versioning Vite Manifest and dev-server tags, CDN base URLs, prefetching and CSP nonces Vite Server-side rendering Render the first visit on Node or Bun, supervised by the app, with a fallback to client rendering SSR CSRF The XSRF-TOKEN cookie and X-XSRF-TOKEN header, configured for you CSRF Multiple apps Mount a second Inertia UI under its own path with its own shared props and root view Mounts Native AOT Minimal API apps publish as Native AOT, using source-generated JSON metadata Native AOT TypeScript Generate declarations for page props, shared props and flash data from .NET types TypeScript types Testing Fluent assertions over Inertia responses, with helpers for partial reloads and deferred props Testing DevTools Record visits for the Inertia DevTools extension and catch missing page components DevTools Prop features Props are the data a page receives, and most of the performance and user-experience features of Inertia are choices about how a prop is sent. Prop type In C What it does Learn more --- --- --- --- Plain ["title"] = "Hi" Sent on every response that includes the key Props Lazy Prop(() = ...) The loader runs only when the prop is part of the response Props Always Always(value) Sent even when a partial reload does not ask for it Partial reloads Optional Optional(() = ...) Never sent on the first visit, only when a partial reload asks for it Partial reloads Deferred Defer(() = ..., group: "stats") Left out of the first response, then loaded right away so the page shows up sooner Deferred props Merge Merge(value) , DeepMerge(value) The client appends or deep merges new data instead of replacing it Merging props Once Once(() = ...) Resolved once and remembered by the client, with optional expiry Once props Infinite scroll Scroll(page, ...) Merges pages of items and reports paging metadata Infinite scroll Rescued .Rescue() If its loader throws, the prop is left out and reported in rescuedProps instead of failing the whole page Props Parallel .Parallel() Starts independent async loaders together instead of one after another Props Cached .Cache(key, duration) Caches a loader's result between requests Props Live live props Refresh themselves when the server broadcasts an event, over SignalR or your own transport Live props Partial reloads let the client ask for only some props ( only and except ), so a filter change or a poll does not recompute the whole page. See Pagination for the numbered and cursor pages that feed pagers and infinite scroll. When it is not a good fit - You need a public API anyway. Mobile apps, third-party integrations or several different clients need real JSON endpoints. You can build those next to your Inertia pages, but Inertia will not replace them. - The frontend is a separate product. If another team deploys the frontend on its own schedule, a versioned API is the cleaner boundary. - Heavy offline use. Inertia expects the server for every page change. - You want no JavaScript at all. For server-rendered HTML with a little interactivity, Razor Pages or Blazor may be simpler. What it is not Inertia is not a framework and not a new frontend library. It is a small protocol between your server and the official Inertia.js client, and Inertia.Net is the ASP.NET Core side of it. You keep using React, Vue or Svelte exactly as documented. Next steps - First 10 minutes creates an app from the starter template and walks through a validated form. - Quick start adds Inertia.Net to an existing ASP.NET Core app. - Introduction summarizes what the adapter provides.

title: Error pages
description: Render routing failures and unhandled exceptions as Inertia pages, with shared props and the original status.
body: When someone visits a missing page or the server encounters an error, you can show a page from your app instead of a blank response. Add this setup in Program.cs for production: A second Inertia UI mounted under its own path registers its own components with AddInertiaErrorPages(name, ...) ; see Multiple apps and libraries. Create the named components in your client pages directory. Each receives status , the optional Props callback's values, and shared props registered globally or through context.Inertia().Share(...) . The callback receives the exception for exception responses and null for status-code pages. Avoid returning exception messages or stack traces to the client. For example, ClientApp/pages/Error.tsx ( Error.vue for Vue, Error.svelte for Svelte): The handler answers requests with X-Inertia or an Accept: text/html navigation. It preserves the error status: XHR receives a JSON page with X-Inertia: true ; the first visit receives the normal root template. Root views and SSR work as for any other render. An error component must also resolve in your SSR bundle when SSR is enabled. Only configured error statuses with an empty response are replaced. API clients, existing response bodies, redirects, Inertia's 409 responses and antiforgery's 419 responses are left to their existing handlers. Exceptions use the status selected by ASP.NET Core's exception middleware (500 by default). The default statuses are 403, 404, 500 and 503; extend StatusCodes to handle other error statuses. A page explicitly returned with Render(...).WithStatusCode(404) keeps its component and props. In Development, error pages are disabled so the developer exception page and Inertia debug modal stay available. Set o.EnabledInDevelopment = true to preview your error components. The Inertia client renders non-2xx Inertia responses by default; application httpException event handlers or onHttpException callbacks can cancel that rendering. Already using UseExceptionHandler() AddInertiaErrorPages() registers an IExceptionHandler in the existing chain. Register API-specific handlers first if they should take priority. Use one exception middleware, then install just the status-code part: ASP.NET Core 10 suppresses exception diagnostics by default when an IExceptionHandler handles the exception. The Inertia handler follows that policy and emits only a Debug message naming the rendered component. To keep the built-in exception logs and diagnostics, configure the exception middleware explicitly: AddInertiaErrorPages() also registers the built-in ProblemDetails service as the exception middleware’s fallback. The Inertia exception handler declines requests that do not ask for an Inertia page or HTML, so API exceptions use the host’s ProblemDetails fallback and content negotiation. Existing ProblemDetails configuration and earlier application handlers still apply; empty status-code responses remain unchanged. Loaded flash and validation state is consumed when an error page renders, as on any other page response. Validation, SSR and rate limits Validation redirects keep their existing behavior. A required SSR failure can be handled by the exception pipeline; configure the error page so it can render without relying on the same failed renderer. Rate-limit responses with an existing body are preserved; configure the rejection response explicitly, including the Precognition header for validation requests. See Precognition.

title: CSRF protection
description: Protect forms with the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and the X-XSRF-TOKEN header.
body: The Inertia client reads the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and sends its value as the X-XSRF-TOKEN header on every request. UseInertiaAntiforgery() issues that cookie and validates it, so one call protects every form. What it does - Issue. Page loads (GET/HEAD requests that are Inertia requests or accept text/html ) get the request token in a script-readable, essential cookie ( HttpOnly off, SameSite=Lax , Path=/ , Secure per SecurePolicy ). Essential means a cookie-consent policy does not withhold it. - Validate. Every unsafe request (anything but GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE), with a JSON or a form body, Inertia or not, is checked with IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync . A plain cross-site HTML form post is rejected as well as a forged XHR. It also sets the antiforgery feature, so form-binding endpoints work without app.UseAntiforgery() . - Reject. A missing or wrong token gets 419 (page expired, as in Laravel); the handler does not run. - Opt out per endpoint with .DisableAntiforgery() (webhooks, test hooks), or for whole areas with ShouldValidate . .NET 11 automatic CSRF check Apps built with WebApplication.CreateBuilder on .NET 11 also get the framework's automatic CSRF middleware. It checks Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin on unsafe requests, issues no tokens, and only records a verdict. UseInertiaAntiforgery() remains the token check Inertia needs: like app.UseAntiforgery() , it replaces that verdict with its own, so a request with a valid token passes and one without still gets 419 . .DisableAntiforgery() opts an endpoint out of both; configuration DisableCsrfProtection=true turns the automatic check off. Options OnRejected runs after UseInertia() ; returning Back() gives the tab a fresh token and a message instead of the client's error dialog. Lazy refresh By default every page load issues a fresh token, and antiforgery marks that response Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store (which also keeps the page out of the browser's back/forward cache). o.CookieRefresh = XsrfCookieRefresh.Lazy keeps a token that still validates. Such responses get no Set-Cookie and stay cacheable, and a token issued before a sign-in or sign-out is replaced on the next page load. Validating costs about what issuing does, so the gain is in the responses, not in CPU. Set your own Cache-Control on pages with private data. A session that expires or a sign-in that changes the user invalidates the token in an open tab; the next page load issues a new one. Returning Back() from OnRejected gives that tab a fresh token and a message. MVC and FastEndpoints UseInertiaAntiforgery() covers controllers too. [AutoValidateAntiforgeryToken] as a global filter still works, but is not needed. FastEndpoints is covered by the middleware; FastEndpoints' own EnableAntiforgery() is not needed for Inertia forms. Issue only UseInertiaAntiforgeryCookie(cookieName = "XSRF-TOKEN") (the 1.0 API) only writes the cookie. You then validate with app.UseAntiforgery() (form bodies only) and your own check for JSON bodies ( await antiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync(context) ). Prefer UseInertiaAntiforgery() . Troubleshooting 419 - Was the page loaded through the middleware? It sets the cookie. - Does the cookie reach the browser? Secure cookies are dropped on plain HTTP; behind a TLS-terminating proxy, configure forwarded headers or set CookieSecurePolicy.Always . - Do all instances share the Data Protection key ring? - Does UseAuthentication() run before the antiforgery middleware? - Did a sign-in or sign-out change the token? Reload the page, or use OnRejected . See Deploying for proxy and multi-instance settings.

title: Server-side rendering
description: Render the first visit on Bun or Node, supervise the process from .NET, and fall back safely.
headings: 3. Let the app run Bun or Node
body: SSR renders the first visit on a JavaScript server using your client bundle, so crawlers and slow devices get HTML. Inertia XHR requests are never rendered on the server. 1. Build the SSR bundle With @inertiajs/vite The plugin wraps the entry with the SSR server bootstrap and resolves your pages. The entry is ClientApp/ssr.tsx for React and ClientApp/ssr.ts for Vue and Svelte. Build both bundles: Without the plugin Write the server entry yourself ( ssr.tsx for React, ssr.ts for Vue and Svelte): The client entry hydrates when the server rendered: Run the bundle with Bun or Node, or let the app start it: Build and run from a directory with node modules installed. The SSR build leaves node modules imports external. 2. Enable it A response can choose its own mode: The global mode decides first: Disabled is a kill switch no response can override. Otherwise the response's mode wins, then ExcludePaths , then the global mode. SSR runs only for first visits (the HTML response). The page JSON is posted to {url}/render , and { "head": [...], "body": "..." } is written into the root view. @inertiaHead outputs the head tags; @inertia outputs the body. 3. Let the app run Bun or Node A hosted service runs {Executable} {bundle} ( node by default; Bun works too) once per instance, logs stdout as Information and stderr as Warning under Inertia.Net.Ssr , and waits for every instance's GET /health . Occupied ports are refused before anything is spawned. Ssr.Urls is not used in managed mode. The executable is configurable. This documentation site builds a self-contained SSR bundle and runs it with Bun: o.Ssr.UseNodeProcess(n = n.Executable = "bun") . The default is node ; the bundle accepts either runtime. - An instance that exits is restarted after 1 second, doubling to 30 seconds. - An instance that stops answering its liveness check is killed and restarted the same way. - Shutdown stops the owned process trees without requesting /shutdown . - Nothing is spawned while the Vite dev server runs. - For external or remote servers, set Mode and Urls without UseNodeProcess() . The SSR server has no authentication. Anyone who can reach it can POST /render (CPU) or POST /shutdown , and its head and body are written into your pages verbatim. Listen on 127.0.0.1 . Before an instance takes renders, Inertia.Net tries the machine's non-loopback addresses on its port. If the instance answers there, it is stopped and an error is logged. AllowNetworkExposure = true keeps it running with a warning. A graceful shutdown stops the SSR process. If the .NET process is killed outright, the OS does not take the runtime with it. Use a process manager or container for hard-crash cleanup. 4. Development With the Vite hot file present (Development only), or o.Vite.DevServerUrl set, Inertia.Net posts to {viteDevUrl}/ inertia ssr . The endpoint is served by @inertiajs/vite , so you need no built bundle and no separate SSR server. Use ssr.ts as the entry for Vue and Svelte. BundlePath is ignored while the dev server runs. 5. Failures and fallbacks In Preferred mode every failure logs a warning and the page renders on the client. In Required mode it throws InertiaSsrException before the first byte is written, so the app's exception handler can still answer. After enough failures in a row the app stops calling the server for a while, then probes it before trusting it again: Type Cause Opens the circuit --- --- --- connection Connection refused or reset. A refused connection is retried on another server. yes timeout Ssr.Timeout elapsed yes http Non-2xx answer without a structured error yes response Empty or malformed answer yes render The component threw (structured error from the renderer) no response-too-large Answer over MaxResponseBytes no overloaded No render slot within Concurrency.QueueTimeout , or the queue is full no circuit-open , not-ready , page-too-large , bundle-missing Skipped without a call no Circuit breaker. After CircuitBreaker.FailureThreshold (default 5) consecutive failures that open the circuit, a server is skipped for BreakDuration (default 10 s). Then one render probes it: success closes the circuit, failure starts another break. A page that fails because of its own code never pauses the server. Render slots. Each server takes at most Concurrency.MaxActive renders at once (default 8, 0 for no limit) from this app instance, with up to MaxQueued (default 32) waiting at most QueueTimeout (default 250 ms). Renders that find no slot fall back immediately. 6. Several servers Each render goes to the server with the fewest renders in flight among those whose circuit is closed (ties rotate). Every server has its own slots, queue and circuit. Only a refused connection is retried on another server within the same deadline. Page props travel to the renderer, and its HTML goes into your pages unescaped, so it must be trusted. A plain http:// URL that is not loopback logs a warning at startup. Use HTTPS or a private network. 7. Health check The check reports what the renders have already shown, without calling the SSR servers: healthy while SSR is disabled, goes through the Vite dev server, or every server can take renders; degraded while some circuits are open or some managed instances are not ready; the registration's failure status (default unhealthy) when none can. Its data lists each server's state. 8. Observability Instrument Type Tags --- --- --- inertia.page.duration (s) histogram inertia.response , inertia.partial inertia.page.size (By) histogram inertia.response inertia.ssr.duration (s) histogram inertia.ssr.outcome inertia.ssr.queue.duration (s) histogram inertia.ssr.active up-down counter inertia.ssr.outcomes counter inertia.ssr.outcome , inertia.ssr.reason inertia.ssr.response.size (By) histogram inertia.ssr.circuit.state gauge inertia.ssr.endpoint inertia.ssr.circuit.transitions counter inertia.ssr.endpoint , to inertia.ssr.process.restarts counter cause inertia.props.rescued counter Tag values are bounded: no URLs, component names or user data. The inertia.render activity carries inertia.component ; the inertia.ssr activity carries inertia.ssr.endpoint , inertia.ssr.outcome and inertia.ssr.reason . Nothing is recorded unless a listener is attached. 9. Response cache A render depends only on the page JSON, so a page that many visitors see byte for byte the same can reuse its HTML: The key is the SHA-256 of the page JSON (component, props, url, version and the rest), so a new deploy or different props never reuse a stale render. Pages with per-user props make one entry per user; cache the pages that are shared. A hit is counted as inertia.ssr.outcomes{inertia.ssr.outcome=rendered, inertia.ssr.reason=cache} and bypasses the render slots and circuit breakers. Nothing is cached while the Vite dev server renders. Concurrent misses for the same page share one fill per app instance. Waiting counts against Ssr.Timeout ; cancelling a waiting request does not cancel the request filling the entry. With StaleFor , a render past its Duration is still served and refreshed by the bounded background worker after response completion, like stale props. The connection can accept its next request while the renderer runs. Refreshes cancel when the host stops. If the 64-entry queue is full, the refresh is dropped and logged; monitor inertia.cache.refresh.dropped with inertia.cache.kind=ssr . IInertiaCache.ClearSsrAsync() removes every render. Ssr.ConnectTimeout bounds connection establishment independently of Ssr.Timeout ; both accept a positive duration or Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan . In Required mode, InertiaSsrException.Message contains a generic failure category suitable for an error page. Renderer diagnostics remain in application logs and diagnostic exception properties; do not expose those properties to clients. Connection timeout and cached renders Ssr.ConnectTimeout defaults to five seconds and limits connection establishment; Ssr.Timeout bounds the entire render. In Required mode, exceptions use a generic public message; diagnostic properties can contain private renderer details, so do not display them to users. A stale SSR cache hit returns immediately and schedules refresh on a bounded background worker. Its queue holds 64 pending refreshes; a dropped refresh logs a warning and increments inertia.cache.refresh.dropped with inertia.cache.kind=ssr . Cached prop loaders used with stale refresh must use singleton dependencies or create their own scope; never capture request-scoped services or HttpContext . Global Ssr.Cache.Duration is suitable for anonymous pages. Prefer per-page WithSsrCache and keys that account for all user and tenant data.

title: Validation
description: Redirect back with validation errors for Minimal APIs, MVC and FastEndpoints, and add Precognition.
body: Inertia forms post, expect a redirect, and read validation errors from props.errors on the next page. Inertia.Net performs the redirect and carries the errors across it. - A field maps to its first message. With o.WithAllErrors = true it maps to an array of all messages (the client's form.withAllErrors() expects that). - Error keys use dotted indices, for example items.0.email . Names use JSON member aliases when metadata exposes them and the applicable naming policy for other members. Dictionary keys are preserved. Minimal API and MVC use the page serializer’s HTTP JSON options; FastEndpoints uses its binding serializer policy. Custom resolvers that omit member metadata and paths without a model schema may fall back to naming-policy conversion; align field names and serializer settings. - Error bags. The client sends X-Inertia-Error-Bag: createUser when the form has errorBag="createUser" . Errors arrive as errors: { createUser: { email: "..." } } . Without the header, errors is the flat object { email: "..." } . A bag stored under a name other than default is always nested by bag name. Validation libraries Backend Validation --- --- Minimal API .NET 10 source-generated DataAnnotations through AddValidation() ; ValidationProblem results; call FluentValidation IValidator manually and return WithErrors MVC MVC model validation and ModelState FastEndpoints FastEndpoints validators, including FluentValidation Minimal API WithInertiaValidation() applies to a route or route group and requires services.AddValidation() . Without validation resolvers, it throws InvalidOperationException when the endpoint is constructed. Routing may construct endpoints lazily, so this need not happen during application startup. For an Inertia request that is not a GET, a failure becomes a redirect back (303 for PUT/PATCH/DELETE) with the errors. Every other client still gets the normal 400 validation problem. A handler that returns TypedResults.ValidationProblem(...) , Results.ValidationProblem(...) or an HttpValidationProblemDetails is converted the same way. On .NET 11, async validators ( AsyncValidationAttribute , IAsyncValidatableObject ) report through WithInertiaValidation() and WithInertiaPrecognition() like synchronous attributes. A body that cannot be bound (malformed JSON) is still a 400 on both .NET 10 and .NET 11, never a redirect back without errors or a Precognition success. The built-in .NET 10 validation filter is added automatically and always runs outermost: it writes the 400 itself before any filter you add can see it. WithInertiaValidation() disables it on the endpoint and runs the same source-generated validation itself. Do not combine it with your own .DisableValidation() . To report errors yourself, without attribute validation: Back().WithErrors(IDictionary errors, string bag = "default") also takes arrays of messages. FluentValidation is not automatically integrated into Minimal API AddValidation() . Call a registered IValidator yourself and map its failures: Import FluentValidation and register your validator. Supply client JSON field names in the dictionary when they differ from its property names. MVC AddInertiaMvc() registers a global filter. An Inertia non-GET request with an invalid ModelState is redirected back with the errors before the action runs, in the bag from X-Inertia-Error-Bag (default default ). [ApiController] controllers work too: their automatic 400 is replaced by the same redirect for Inertia requests. Binding failures get the generic message The value is invalid. , because their exception messages can expose internals. FastEndpoints c.ConfigureInertia() adds a global pre-processor. A validation failure of an Inertia non-GET request becomes a redirect back with the errors; other requests keep FastEndpoints' 400 JSON. FluentValidation validators work as usual. c.ConfigureInertia() composes with an existing c.Endpoints.Configurator . Its optional callback runs after Inertia setup. The pre-processor runs after an endpoint's own pre-processors, so one that already answered (a 403, say) wins. Precognition (live validation) Precognition validates a request without running the handler. Minimal APIs use .WithInertiaPrecognition() instead of .WithInertiaValidation() ; FastEndpoints enables it with ConfigureInertia() . MVC does not support it. Error bags in the client All errors for a field With the option on, errors.email is an array of every message instead of the first. State and redirects Validation errors travel in the state store across the redirect. By default that is an encrypted cookie; it can be a session or MVC TempData instead. See Flash data for the store choices and size limits.

title: Native AOT
description: Publish a Native AOT Inertia.Net app with source-generated JSON metadata.
body: Inertia.Net , Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints and Inertia.Net.Live.SignalR are annotated IsAotCompatible . A real app is published with Native AOT in CI ( tests/Inertia.Net.AotSmoke ) with zero trim and AOT warnings allowed. The library never reflects over your props: values are written with JsonTypeInfo from your JsonSerializerContext . 1. Register a JSON context Register every prop type and chain the context into the HTTP JSON options: Register the type that each loader returns and each plain value you place in InertiaProps , plus flash values that are not plain strings or numbers. The library's own context already covers string , bool , int , long , double , decimal , float , Guid , DateTime , DateTimeOffset , DateOnly , TimeOnly , TimeSpan , JsonElement , string[] , int[] , List , Dictionary , Dictionary , InertiaProps and Dictionary . Members of type InertiaProp are accepted by the source generator without any attribute. 2. Make validation models public The .NET 10 AddValidation() source generator skips internal types, and validation then silently does nothing. Only one AddValidation() call site per project is allowed. 3. Add ProblemDetails The non-Inertia 400 validation problem needs the ProblemDetails JSON metadata, or it cannot be serialized without reflection. 4. Avoid anonymous types Anonymous types do not work as props, flash values or published live prop values under AOT. Use InertiaProps , records or classes registered in the context, and register the types you publish as live values in the same context. 5. Copy content files app.html and the Vite manifest are read from disk at runtime. Copy them to the publish directory, and set the content root to the binary's directory when it may run from elsewhere: 6. Use Minimal APIs or FastEndpoints MVC is not AOT compatible (neither is MVC itself), so Inertia.Net.Mvc is not either. Use Minimal APIs or FastEndpoints. 7. FastEndpoints source generation DiscoveredTypes is generated by the FastEndpoints.Generator package, in the namespace named after the assembly. See samples/FastEndpoints.Svelte . 8. Trim HTTP/3 The SSR client never uses HTTP/3, so it can be trimmed out: Cached props, the SSR cache, nonces, prefetching, MapInertia , the DevTools recorder and live props over SignalR are all AOT safe and covered by the smoke test. SignalR itself does not support strongly typed hubs ( Hub ) under AOT, so keep any hubs of your own untyped. Set JsonSerializerIsReflectionEnabledByDefault=false in regular builds too. A missing JsonSerializable registration then fails in tests instead of only in the AOT publish. The reference app is tests/Inertia.Net.AotSmoke/Program.cs . Run it end to end with bash eng/aot-smoke.sh on Linux with clang and zlib installed.

title: Troubleshooting
description: Common errors, their causes, and how to fix them.
headings: My 404 shows the Inertia modal in production
The Inertia page component was not found
A redirect to another site turns into a 409
The root view resolves outside the content root
The page keeps reloading, or a request loops with 409
The dev server tags do not appear
The root template was not found, or @inertia is missing
Validation errors do not show up (Minimal API)
Validation keys do not match my field names
InertiaProp values can only be serialized by Inertia.Net
Native AOT: JsonTypeInfo metadata was not provided
SSR does not run and there is no error
Several managed instances never become healthy
The SSR output is not hydrated
Does it work behind a path base?
Can I mix Razor Pages or views with Inertia pages?
Precognition: login locks users out while typing
